title: Show HN: Replay your Claude Code logs to count parallel session collisions
author: dooly6276
body:
# dooly6276/claude-bulkhead Run many Claude Code sessions on one machine safely: no killed dev servers, port clashes, RAM or disk freezes, or mixed-up commits. Zero-dependency hooks. - Stars: 20 - Forks: 3 - Watchers: 20 - Open issues: 0 - License: MIT License - Default branch: main - Created: 2026-10-13T03:58:13Z ## Languages - JavaScript - Shell ## Topics - agentic-coding - ai-agents - anthropic - claude - claude-code - claude-code-hooks - claude-code-plugin - developer-tools - git-worktree - hooks - linux - macos - multi-agent - parallel-agents - subagents - windows ## Top Contributors - dooly6276 (15 contributions) - dependabot[bot] (2 contributions) --- ## README English | 한국어 | 简体中文 | 日本語 | Español | Português (Brasil) claude-bulkhead Hooks that stop parallel Claude Code sessions on one machine from killing each other's servers or running it out of RAM. 8 guards, 10 commands, a status line, 6 slash commands, 1 skill, zero dependencies What is it | Scan | Why | Features | Install | Quick start | Remote | How it works | Guards | FAQ > **New in 0.2.0:** `bulkhead scan` replays your past Claude Code sessions against the guards, a new disk-guard stops whole-disk and parallel scans, checkout-guard now stops `git add -A` from sweeping another session's edits into your commit and `rm -rf` of a folder another session works in, and basics stops commits authored as Claude. Release notes: CHANGELOG.md. ## What is it? Claude Code hooks are small programs that Claude Code runs at fixed points, for example before every shell command, and that can stop the command and tell Claude why. bulkhead is a set of these hooks for one situation: several Claude Code sessions, and their subagents, working on the same computer at the same time. Each session acts as if it had the machine to itself. bulkhead checks each shell command against what the other sessions are doing: which processes and ports belong to which session, how much RAM is left, and which git tree each session works in. When a command would hurt another session, it is blocked, and Claude gets a message with the safer command to run instead. **You need it if** you run two or more Claude Code sessions at once, often one per git worktree, or your sessions and subagents start dev servers, builds and test runs. **You probably do not need it if** you run one session at a time and do not let it start servers or builds. Most of what bulkhead does is about sessions getting in each other's way. | Without bulkhead | With bulkhead | |---|---| | An agent restarts its dev server with `pkill node`, and every other worktree's server dies with it. | kill-guard blocks the command and tells the agent how to find and stop its own PID. | | Two worktrees run `npm run dev`. The second moves to 3001, but its agent keeps testing `localhost:3000` and sees the other branch. | port-guard blocks the second start and names a free port. `bulkhead port` prints one on demand. | | Three sessions start `next build`, `npm test` and Playwright in the same minute, and the machine freezes. | memory-guard blocks heavy commands when RAM is low. Through `bulkhead-slot`, the third job waits in a queue until there is room. | | A session checks out another branch in a tree that a second session is editing. | checkout-guard blocks it and suggests `git worktree add`. | | A session exits, and its dev servers, test workers and watchers keep running and holding RAM and ports. | orphan-reaper stops them within seconds of the session exiting. | | A subagent polls in the foreground for ten minutes. The session cannot answer you, and the prompt cache expires. | wait-guard blocks the loop and asks for `run_in_background: true`. | | An agent wants to know what is using disk space and runs ten `du` at once over your home folder. Every session's builds and `git status` crawl for minutes. | disk-guard blocks it and asks for one folder at a time. | | Two sessions share a checkout. One runs `git add -A && git commit`, and the other one's half-finished edits ship in that commit. | checkout-guard blocks it and asks for the file names. | | A "clean up the worktrees" task runs `git worktree remove` on a worktree a second session is still working in. | checkout-guard blocks it and names the session that is still there. | ## Do you need it? Ask your transcripts You do not have to guess. Claude Code keeps every session's transcript in `~/.claude/projects`, and `bulkhead scan` replays the shell commands in them against the guards: how many sessions you really run at once, and how often they already did the things bulkhead blocks. ``` /plugin install bulkhead@bulkhead # then, inside Claude Code: /bulkhead:scan 30d ``` It only reads, masks anything that looks like a secret before printing, and sends nothing anywhere. port-guard and the low-RAM check are not replayed, because transcripts do not record which ports and how much RAM were in use; checkout-guard is rebuilt from which sessions were active in the same git tree at that minute. Details: docs/commands.md. ## Why this exists A common way to speed up work with Claude Code is to run several sessions on one repository, each in its own git worktree, each with its own subagents. git keeps the branches apart. The machine does not: every session shares the same ports, the same process table and the same RAM. That is where they collide. - Two worktrees of the same app both run `npm run dev`. The second one fails on port 3000, or quietly moves to 3001 while its agent keeps testing `localhost:3000` and sees the other branch. - An agent restarts its own server with `pkill node` or `taskkill /IM node.exe` and takes down the dev servers and test runs of every other worktree, and sometimes its own session. - Three sessions start `npm test`, `next build` and a Playwright run in the same minute, and the machine stops responding. - A session ends and the dev servers it started keep running. The Claude Code tracker has many reports of exactly this: - #13941: asked to restart a dev server, Claude ran `taskkill //IM node.exe` or `pkill node` and killed its own session. - #34754: `taskkill //F //IM python.exe` killed two long-running simulations, after the user had marked their PIDs as off limits. - #43225: asked to restart one bot, Claude force-killed every Python process on the machine, about 20 services. - #53229: told to stop only unused dev servers, an agent also killed a gateway and a Postgres process it had not identified. - #15487: 24 subagent processes saturated a 4 GB VPS until it had to be rebooted; a commenter froze a 24 GB Mac the same way. - #11502 and #25180: processes started by agents outlive them, 60 Node processes in one report and 550 pytest workers in the other. claude-bulkhead is a set of small hooks that block or clean up each of these. Each one can be turned off on its own. The name is from the bulkhead pattern: one compartment taking on water should not sink the ship. ## What it does | | | |---|---| | **kill-guard** Blocks `pkill node`, `taskkill /IM`, `Stop-Process -Name` and other kills by program name. Kills by PID pass. | **port-guard** Blocks starting a dev server on a port another session already serves, and killing that session's server by port. | | **memory-guard and bulkhead-slot** Blocks heavy commands when RAM is low, and queues heavy jobs against one RAM budget shared by every session. | **checkout-guard** Blocks `git checkout`, `stash`, `reset --hard`, `git add -A` and similar when another live session works in the same tree, and deleting a folder another session works in. | | **wait-guard** Blocks foreground sleep loops longer than 3 minutes, which make the next request rewrite the whole prompt cache. | **orphan-reaper** When a session exits, stops the dev servers, test workers, watchers and headless browsers it left running. | | **disk-guard** new Blocks `du -sh ~`, `find /` without `-maxdepth`, and disk scans run in parallel, which stall the disk every session shares. | **`bulkhead scan`** new Replays your past Claude Code transcripts against the guards: what they would have stopped, and how many sessions ran at once. | | **basics** Blocks `rm -rf` at a root, home or a folder directly in it, force-pushes to `main`, resets that would lose uncommitted work, and commits authored as Claude. | **`bulkhead status`, `top`, `log`, `doctor`** Shows every session, its RAM, its ports, queued jobs, and what the guards have blocked. | | **Status line** `3 sessions 2 heavy 9.1 GB free` in the Claude Code status line, in under 100 ms. | **Config and slash commands** Per-machine and per-project config with allow lists, plus `/bulkhead:scan`, `/bulkhead:status`, `/bulkhead:log`, `/bulkhead:doctor` and `/bulkhead:reap`. | Optional: **`bulkhead remote`** runs a test suite, a build or a browser run on another machine over SSH, when this one has no RAM to spare. ## Demo bulkhead status, then port-guard, kill-guard and wait-guard blocking an agent Recorded with docs/demo.sh. The two sessions are stand-in processes named `claude`; everything printed comes from the hook scripts and `bulkhead status`. ## Install ``` /plugin marketplace add dooly6276/claude-bulkhead /plugin install bulkhead@bulkhead ``` Node 18 or later must be on `PATH`. The native Claude Code installer does not install Node, so check with `node --version` first. Without Node every hook fails to start: nothing is blocked, and Claude Code shows a `hook error` notice for each hook on every tool call. There are no other dependencies. ## Quick start 1. Install the plugin as above and start a new Claude Code session. 2. See what it would have caught: run `/bulkhead:scan 30d`, or `bulkhead scan` in the Bash tool. It reads your last month of transcripts and changes nothing. 3. Check the setup. Inside Claude Code run `/bulkhead:doctor`, or run `bulkhead doctor` in the Bash tool. Every line should say `OK`. A `WARN` or `FAIL` line names the guard and the reason. 4. Open a terminal next to your sessions and run `bulkhead top` to watch sessions, RAM, ports and heavy jobs live. Press `q` to quit. After that there is nothing to do. The guards run on every Bash and PowerShell call. To see what they stopped, run `bulkhead log` or `/bulkhead:log`; `bulkhead log --summary` counts blocks per guard on your machine. To change a threshold or allow a command, see docs/configuration.md. All commands are listed in docs/commands.md. ## Run heavy jobs on another machine (optional) When several sessions run test suites and builds at once, one machine runs out of RAM: memory-guard blocks the commands, or bulkhead-slot makes them queue. If you have a second machine that is mostly idle, `bulkhead remote` runs the heavy command there instead. ``` bulkhead remote add buildbox dev@192.168.1.20 --ssh-option=IdentityFile=~/.ssh/buildbox bulkhead remote run -- npm test ``` ``` [bulkhead remote] buildbox: 3f2a1c9 already there, 3 changed files (24 KB), 1 deleted [bulkhead remote] buildbox copy a /home/dev/bulkhead-remote/acme-web-3f9a1c port 7172 ...test output... [bulkhead remote] exit 0 after 1m 12s (copy a) ``` - **What is sent.** The current commit as a git bundle (only the commits the remote does not have yet) and your uncommitted changes, deletions included. Ignored files stay here unless you name them with `--files`. Nothing outside the repository is sent. - **Where it runs.** In one of up to 8 copies of the repository on the remote, so parallel runs do not share a working tree. `node_modules` is kept between runs. Each run gets its own port in `$BULKHEAD_PORT`. - **Room.** Locks on the remote hold a copy and a job slot, and `--gb=N` waits until N GB is free there. When there is no room within `--wait` minutes, it exits 3. - **Cleanup.** When the command ends, or the SSH connection drops (Ctrl-C, a tool timeout), everything it started on the remote is stopped, including a server left on its port. - **The remote** needs only an SSH server, `bash`, `git` and `tar`. Linux, macOS and Windows with Git for Windows all work. `bulkhead remote fetch PATH` brings files back from the copy the last run used, and `bulkhead remote status` shows each remote's free RAM and running jobs. In Claude Code, `/bulkhead:remote ` runs a command there in the background. Setup, options and exit codes: docs/remote.md. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR CC["Claude Code session"] -->|"PreToolUse: Bash, PowerShell"| G["kill-guard, wait-guard, memory-guard,
port-guard, checkout-guard, disk-guard, basics"] CC -->|"SessionEnd, SessionStart"| R["orphan-reaper (background)"] G -->|"read"| P["process table, listening ports,
~/.claude/sessions"] G <-->|"read, append"| S[("state dir ~/.claude/bulkhead
slots, guards.log, events.jsonl")] B["bulkhead-slot"] <--> S G -->|"exit 2 + message: blocked"| CC G -->|"exit 0: allowed"| CC G -.->|"any error: exit 0"| CC ``` Each guard is a separate Node script with no dependencies. Claude Code pipes the tool call to it as JSON. The guard reads the command text, and only when the command matches does it look further: at the process table, the listening ports, the session files Claude Code keeps in `~/.claude/sessions`, free RAM, or `git status`. A block is exit code 2 with a message that tells Claude what to do instead. Any error inside a guard lets the call through, so a broken guard never stops your work. Every session on the machine shares one state directory. bulkhead-slot keeps its RAM reservations there, and every block is recorded there. More detail, including the state directory layout and how sessions are found on each OS, is in docs/architecture.md. ## Guards Each guard has a page with the exact commands it blocks, what passes, the message Claude sees, and its limits. The short version: kill-guard: kills by program name Blocks `taskkill /IM`, `taskkill /FI` without a PID, `Stop-Process -Name`, `Get-Process node | Stop-Process`, `pkill`, `killall`, `kill $(pgrep node)`, `wmic ... delete` and similar when they target a program other sessions share, such as `node`, `python`, `java`, `chrome`, `git` or `vite`. Kills by PID and by project path pass. Kills by port pass too, unless another session owns the port; port-guard checks those. Claude is told how to find its own PIDs. Turn off: `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=kill-guard`. Details: docs/guards/kill-guard.md. port-guard: ports owned by another session Blocks starting a dev server (`npm run dev`, `next dev`, `vite`, `uvicorn`, `rails s` and more) on a port that another Claude session's process tree is listening on, and suggests a free port. It also blocks kill-by-port commands such as `npx kill-port 3000`, `fuser -k 3000/tcp` and `lsof -ti :3000 | xargs kill` when another session owns that port. Turn off: `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=port-guard`. Details: docs/guards/port-guard.md. memory-guard and bulkhead-slot: RAM memory-guard blocks heavy commands (test runners, `next build`, `tsc`, Gradle, the Android emulator, Playwright, `cargo test`, `docker build` and similar) when free RAM is under 3 GB, or under 15% of RAM on machines with less than 20 GB. `bulkhead-slot run --gb=4 -- ` waits until the shared RAM budget has room, runs the command, and frees the slot when it exits. Turn off: `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=memory-guard`. Details: docs/guards/memory-guard.md. checkout-guard: two sessions in one git tree Blocks `git checkout `, `switch`, `stash`, `reset --hard`, `clean -f`, `rebase`, `merge`, `restore .` and a dirty `pull` when another live session works in the same tree, and suggests `git worktree add`. Also blocks `git add -A`, `git add .` and `git commit -a` there (`stage-all`), which would sweep the other session's half-finished edits into your commit, and `rm -rf` or `git worktree remove` of a folder another live session works in (`remove-session-dir`). On Windows it blocks `git worktree remove --force` on a worktree that holds junctions, which git has followed into the main checkout. Turn off: `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=checkout-guard`, or one rule with `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=stage-all` or `remove-session-dir`. Details: docs/guards/checkout-guard.md. disk-guard: whole-disk and parallel scans Blocks `du`, `ncdu`, `dust`, `ls -R`, `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` and `dir /s` over the whole drive, the home folder or every user's home (`du -sh ~`, `du -sh ~/*`, `ncdu /`), `find /` and `find ~` without `-maxdepth`, and disk scans run in parallel wherever they point: `xargs -P 10 du`, GNU `parallel`, `du ... &` in a loop, `ForEach-Object -Parallel`. One folder at a time passes (`du -sh node_modules`, `du -sh ~/Library/Caches`). Turn off: `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=disk-guard`. Details: docs/guards/disk-guard.md. wait-guard: long foreground waits Blocks a foreground command whose sleeps can add up to more than 180 seconds. The prompt cache expires after about five minutes without a request, so a subagent polling in the foreground rewrites the whole context every time it wakes. Claude is told to run the loop with `run_in_background: true`. Sleeps in a background job (`sleep 600 &`) pass. With the default 120 second tool timeout a wait cannot pass the default limit, so it blocks only when the call raises the timeout. Turn off: `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=wait-guard`, or raise the limit with `BULKHEAD_WAIT_MAX_SEC`. Details: docs/guards/wait-guard.md. orphan-reaper: processes left by sessions that exited When a session exits, a hidden background waiter stops what it started from its tool shells and left running: dev servers and anything else listening on a port, test runners and their workers (Vitest, Jest, Playwright, pytest and xdist, `cargo test`, `go test` and more), watchers such as `tsc --watch` and nodemon, builds such as `next build`, and headless browsers. A pass at session start catches what a crash left behind. Editors, terminals, shared daemons such as Gradle or adb, and anything you started yourself are never touched. `bulkhead reap --dry-run` shows what it would stop and why. Windows, Linux and macOS (macOS tested with fixtures). Turn off: `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=orphan-reaper`. Details: docs/guards/orphan-reaper.md. basics: four mistakes that cannot be undone `rm-root` (`rm -rf` at a root, a top-level folder such as `/srv`, home, a folder directly in home such as `~/Documents`, or above the repository), `force-push-main` (`git push --force` to `main` or `master`; `--force-with-lease` passes), `discard-changes` (`git reset --hard` or `git clean -fd` that would lose uncommitted work) and `agent-author` (`--author="Claude "`, `git config user.name Claude` and the like, so your commits keep counting as yours). Turn off: `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=basics`, or one rule by name. Details: docs/guards/basics.md. ## How bulkhead relates to other hook packs General safety packs protect a session from dangerous commands. For example, claude-forge includes hooks that filter leaked secrets from output, block piped remote scripts and stop destructive SQL, and dcg and cc-safety-net cover destructive shell and git commands broadly. They are worth using. bulkhead covers a different problem: sessions on one machine getting in each other's way through process ownership, ports, shared RAM and a shared git tree. Only its `basics` rules overlap with those packs, and you can turn them off with `BULKHEAD_DISABLE=basics` if another pack already covers them. bulkhead runs alongside other hooks: Claude Code runs every hook that matches a tool call, and the call is stopped if any of them blocks it. ## Configuration The defaults need no setup. To change them, use a config file: `~/.claude/bulkhead/config.json` for the machine, and ` /.claude/bulkhead.json` for one project (found by walking up to the folder with `.git`). Project settings win over the global file. For example, a project that runs `ffmpeg` on purpose and has a slow integration suite: ```json { "killGuard": { "allowNames": ["ffmpeg"] }, "waitGuard": { "limitSeconds": 300 }, "portGuard": { "ignorePorts": [9229] }, "basics": { "protectedBranches": ["main", "release"] } } ``` Every guard can be turned off with `" ": { "enabled": false }`. `bulkhead config` prints every setting, its value and where it came from. A broken file is ignored, the guards keep their defaults, and the session shows one notice at startup. All keys are in docs/configuration.md, and config.example.json sets each of them. Environment variables still work and win over both files. The simplest place for them is the `env` block of `~/.claude/settings.json`. All environment variables | Variable | Default | Same as | |---|---|---| | `BULKHEAD_DISABLE` | empty | Comma-separated guards to turn off: `kill-guard`, `wait-guard`, `memory-guard`, `port-guard`, `checkout-guard`, `disk-guard`, `orphan-reaper`, `basics`, or `all`. Single rules can be turned off too: `rm-root`, `force-push-main`, `discard-changes`, `agent-author`, `stage-all`, `remove-session-dir`. A name here is off whatever the files say | | `BULKHEAD_WAIT_MAX_SEC` | 180 | `waitGuard.limitSeconds` | | `BULKHEAD_MIN_FREE_GB` | 3, or 15% of RAM if less | `memory.minFreeGb` | | `BULKHEAD_SLOT_FLOOR_GB` | 5, or 25% of RAM if less | `memory.slotFloorGb` | | `BULKHEAD_MAX_COMMIT_PCT` | 75 | `memory.maxCommitPct` (Windows only) | | `BULKHEAD_NO_LOG` | empty | `log.enabled: false` when set to `1` | | `BULKHEAD_STATE_DIR` | `~/.claude/bulkhead` | Where slots, the event log, `guards.log` and the global config file live | | `BULKHEAD_SSH` | `ssh` on `PATH` | The ssh client `bulkhead remote` runs | ## See what is running `bulkhead` is on the Bash tool's `PATH` next to `bulkhead-slot`. Inside Claude Code, `/bulkhead:scan [30d]`, `/bulkhead:status`, `/bulkhead:log [24h|7d]`, `/bulkhead:doctor` and `/bulkhead:reap` run the matching command and summarize it. To run it in your own terminal, call it by path, for example `node ~/.claude/plugins/cache/bulkhead/bulkhead/0.2.0/bin/bulkhead top` (the cache path depends on your install; `/plugin` shows it). Every command that prints a table takes `--json`. The full reference is docs/commands.md. ### bulkhead status Every Claude Code session on the machine, the memory its process tree uses, what it has listening on a port, the jobs held in bulkhead-slot and the ones waiting, and free RAM: ``` $ bulkhead status SESSION STARTED RSS PROJECT 18672 Oct 12 17:49 1.4 GB ~/src/acme-web :3000 node.exe pid 24632 21888 Oct 12 17:52 353 MB ~/src/acme-web-auth 26448 03:43 625 MB ~/src/acme-web-checkout :3001 node.exe pid 31020 SLOT GB PID AGE COMMAND slot-1 4 30112 6 min npx playwright test WAITING GB PID FOR COMMAND #1 3 30200 2 min npm run build 9.9 GB free of 31.8 GB, commit 68% ``` `bulkhead slot ...` is the same as `bulkhead-slot ...`. ### bulkhead top The same view, live and full screen. It refreshes every 2 seconds on Linux and macOS and every 4 seconds on Windows, where one process scan takes 1 to 2 seconds. The scan runs in a worker thread, so keys never wait for it. `q`, `Esc` or `Ctrl-C` quit, `r` refreshes. ``` bulkhead top 14:30:05 scan 1.4s every 4s q quit r refresh RAM ████████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ 9.9 GB free of 31.8 GB commit 68% SESSIONS 3 PID STARTED PROJECT RSS PROCS PORTS 18672 Oct 12 17:49 ~/src/acme-web 1.4 GB ██████████ 12 :3000 :24678 21888 Oct 12 17:52 ~/src/acme-web-auth 353 MB ███░░░░░░░ 3 - 26448 03:43 ~/src/acme-web-checkout 625 MB ████░░░░░░ 5 :3001 HEAVY JOBS 1 running, 1 waiting slot-1 4 GB 30112 6 min npx playwright test wait #1 3 GB 30200 2 min npm run build (this machine has 16 GB; one heavy job at a time) RECENT BLOCKS 14:29 kill-guard taskkill-im ~/src/acme-web-auth taskkill /F /IM node.exe 14:12 wait-guard poll-loop ~/src/acme-web-checkout until [ -f out/DONE ]; do sleep 30; done ``` On a narrow terminal it drops columns instead of wrapping. When the output is not a terminal, or with `--once`, it prints one snapshot and exits. ### bulkhead log Every block, and every process orphan-reaper stops, is one JSON line in ` /events.jsonl` with the time, guard, rule, session, project and the command cut to 200 characters. The file stays on your machine, rotates at 1 MB, and keeps one old file. `BULKHEAD_NO_LOG=1` turns it off. ``` $ bulkhead log --summary --since 7d 10 blocks in the last 7 days, 3 projects, 4 sessions GUARD RULE COUNT LAST wait-guard poll-loop 3 06:40 ████████████████████████ wait-guard long-sleep 2 06:40 ████████████████ basics force-push-main 1 06:40 ████████ basics rm-root 1 06:40 ████████ kill-guard pkill 1 06:40 ████████ kill-guard taskkill-im 1 06:40 ████████ memory-guard slot-files 1 06:40 ████████ PROJECT COUNT ~/src/acme-web 4 ~/src/acme-web-auth 3 ~/src/acme-web-checkout 3 ``` `bulkhead log -n 20` lists the events themselves, `--since 30m|24h|7d|2w| ` limits the time, and `--guard kill-guard` limits the guard. ### bulkhead doctor Checks Node, the plugin files, the state directory, the config files, each guard (on or off, and why), a real hook run, the process reader with its timing, the session files, the RAM limits computed for this machine, held slots, the event log and git. The exit code is 1 when any check fails. ``` $ bulkhead doctor OK node v24.11.0 OK plugin ~/.claude/plugins/cache/bulkhead/bulkhead/0.2.0, hooks: 2 SessionStart, 1 SessionEnd, 7 PreToolUse OK state dir ~/.claude/bulkhead is writable OK config no config files, defaults in use OK kill-guard on OK wait-guard on, limit 180s OK memory-guard on OK port-guard on OK checkout-guard on OK disk-guard on OK basics on, protected branches: main, master OK orphan-reaper on, at session start and after each session ends OK hook run kill-guard blocked a test command in 90 ms OK processes 356 processes, 21 listening ports, 8 Claude sessions in 2.4s OK sessions ~/.claude/sessions (8 session files) OK memory 12.2 of 31.8 GB free, commit 43%, memory-guard blocks heavy commands below 3 GB, bulkhead-slot keeps 5 GB free for a second job, and waits while commit is above 75% OK slots none held OK event log ~/.claude/bulkhead/events.jsonl, empty so far OK git 2.52.0.windows.1 19 OK, 0 WARN, 0 FAIL ``` ### bulkhead port Prints a port that nothing listens on, checked on IPv4 and IPv6, so a second worktree can start its server without guessing: ``` npm run dev -- --port $(bulkhead port --near 3000) ``` ### bulkhead reap Runs orphan-reaper now. `--dry-run` lists what it would stop, the rule that matched and why the session counts as exited, without stopping anything: ``` $ bulkhead reap --dry-run would stop 30112 test-runner node ~/src/acme-web/node_modules/vitest/dist/workers/forks.js Vitest and its worker pool (tinypool); its session has exited and removed snapshot-bash-1791860359256-ezwkie.sh; 6 processes from 30080 1 tree would be stopped. Run `bulkhead reap` to stop it. ``` ### Status line `bulkhead-statusline` prints one line for the Claude Code status line: ``` 3 sessions 2 heavy 9.1 GB free ``` Sessions are the live entries in `~/.claude/sessions`, heavy is the number of jobs holding a bulkhead-slot, and free is the same measure memory-guard uses. It does not scan processes, takes under 100 ms, and caches the line for 5 seconds in the state directory. A plugin cannot set the main status line (plugin settings only support `agent` and `subagentStatusLine`), so add it to `~/.claude/settings.json` yourself: ```json { "statusLine": { "type": "command", "command": "node ~/.claude/plugins/cache/bulkhead/bulkhead/0.2.0/bin/bulkhead-statusline", "refreshInterval": 10 } } ``` The path contains the plugin version, so update it after a plugin update. If you already have a status line script, call `bulkhead-statusline` from it and append its output. ## FAQ **Does it slow Claude Code down?** A little. Each guard is one short Node process. On a Windows 11 desktop with Node 24, `node scripts/bench-hooks.js 15` measured 40 to 49 ms per guard on an allowed command (median of 15 runs), and 33 ms for starting Node alone. Writing a block to the event log adds no measurable time. The guards only do slow work, such as reading the process list (a second or two on Windows), when the command matches: a dev server start on a port that already answers, a kill, a heavy command. The status line takes under 100 ms and is cached for 5 seconds. **It blocked something it should not have. What do I do?** Run `bulkhead log` to see the exact command and reason. Let it through in the project config, ` /.claude/bulkhead.json`: `killGuard.allowNames` for a program name, `portGuard.ignorePorts` for a shared port, `waitGuard.limitSeconds` for a longer wait, or `"enabled": false` for the whole guard in that project. See docs/configuration.md. Then please open a false positive issue with the line from `bulkhead log`, so the pattern can be fixed for everyone. **Is it useful with a single session?** Yes. kill-guard, wait-guard, memory-guard and basics protect one session and its subagents just as well. port-guard and checkout-guard only act when another session is alive, and orphan-reaper cleans up after sessions that have exited. **Which systems does it support?** Windows, Linux and macOS, with Node 18 or later. orphan-reaper on macOS is tested with fixtures of `ps` output but not yet on a real Mac, and on Linux it needs a Claude Code version that sets `CLAUDE_PID` for tool shells. On Windows, `bulkhead-slot` runs commands through Git Bash when it is installed and through `cmd.exe` otherwise. **Does it send anything anywhere?** No. There is no telemetry and no network call. The only socket it opens is port-guard's connection attempt to `localhost` to see whether a port answers. Logs stay in the state directory. The one exception is `bulkhead remote`, which connects over SSH to a machine you configured, and only when you run it. More questions, including how the guards can be bypassed and how the RAM numbers are measured, are in docs/faq.md. ## Limitations - The guards read command text. They split it into commands and open wrappers such as `bash -c`, `cmd /c`, `powershell -EncodedCommand` and `sudo` up to three levels deep, but a kill or a sleep hidden in a script file, a shell function or an alias is not seen. They catch the common shapes, not a determined workaround. - memory-guard and bulkhead-slot only see RAM. They do not limit CPU, disk or GPU. - bulkhead-slot is only used when called. Nothing forces every session to queue through it. - Each guard page lists its own limits. ## Uninstall ``` /plugin uninstall bulkhead@bulkhead /plugin marketplace remove bulkhead ``` Then delete the state directory (`~/.claude/bulkhead`, or `BULKHEAD_STATE_DIR` if you set it) and remove the `statusLine` entry from `~/.claude/settings.json` if you added one. ## Using bulkhead? Show it Add this badge to your project's README: ```markdown Guarded by bulkhead ``` It renders as Guarded by bulkhead ## Contributing See CONTRIBUTING.md. Security reports: SECURITY.md. The changelog is in CHANGELOG.md, and what bulkhead stores and sends is in PRIVACY.md. ## License MIT # SafeScript/safescript

author: morrk0r
body:

Free, private, no account
 Ride where the signal ends
 Plan the ride, find the café, follow the turns, and do all of it where the signal ends. Free, no account, and your routes and rides stay with you.
 Download a region once and the whole app works without a network: the map, the routing, the place search and the spoken turns. No account, no ads, no paywall on the ride itself. Your routes and rides stay with you: on your phone, or in your own iCloud or Google Drive when you sync them, and they export any time as GPX, FIT or TCX. No server of ours is in the loop unless you ask for one.
 Get Velorki Read the docs 
 Download on the App Store 
 Get it on Google Play 
 Get it on GitHub 
or plan in your browser → 
Everything on the phone is free
 Planning, loops, offline maps and routing, search, navigation, recording, sensors and the Apple Watch, ride stats, the weather map and the weather along the route, GPX, FIT and TCX files, sync through your own iCloud or Google Drive, and the Strava and Ride with GPS connections — for everyone, for good. The routing data and the search index are mirrored for you at no charge.
 Routing on the phone
 Loops
 Offline search
 Offline maps
 Turn-by-turn
 Recording
 Sensors and watch
 GPX, FIT and TCX
 Sync with your own cloud

 Compatible with Strava and Ride with GPS
What it does
 Seven things you will use on every ride. Every screenshot below is the real app.
 Theme Show the app in Dark Light 
 Accent Volt Ember Glacier Berry Forest 
 The app ships light and dark with five accents. Switching here swaps every screenshot on this page.
Planning
 A route for the bike you are on
 Tap waypoints on the map and the route is calculated on the phone, on downloaded 5°×5° tiles. Touring, road, gravel, MTB and direct profiles, up to three alternatives, the elevation profile and a breakdown of the surfaces you will ride on. The route can be coloured by gradient, surface, wind or rain, and one time slider sets when you leave and moves the weather on the map and along the route.
 Five bike profiles, up to three alternatives per route 
 Elevation profile and surface statistics for every option 
 An online routing server is optional, for areas with no tiles 
Loops
 “A 60 km round trip from here via the lake”
 Say how far you want to ride and, if you like, one place to pass. Candidates are generated on the phone and scored on length, climbing, surface and repeated roads, so what comes back is a ride, not a detour.
 Round trips that come back to where you started 
 Scored on length, climbing, surface and repeated roads 
 Pick a place to pass and the loop goes through it 
Offline
 The map, the routing and the search, with no connection
 Each routing tile brings a search index of its places, streets with house numbers and points of interest: cafés, drinking water, toilets, repair stations, shelters, bike shops, campsites, hotels, passes, peaks, viewpoints, stations and landmarks. Typing “water” lists the nearest taps by distance, and typos are corrected from the index itself.
 Vector map areas saved per region 
 Search by category: cafés, water, toilets, repair stations 
 Online place search is one tap away 
Navigation
 Spoken turns, on the phone
 A turn banner and spoken cues while you ride a route, and when you leave it, your choice of a way back onto the plan, a new route to the destination or just the direction back, all worked out on the phone. Compass or north-up follow modes. The cues are generated from the same routing data that planned the ride, so they work where there is no network. A GPX route brings its own cue sheet and points of interest along, and the record sheet adds an elevation profile with the climb ahead, the arrival time and the cue list as swipeable pages. A GPX without turns gets them created on the phone from the map.
 Turn banner and voice cues, offline 
 Leave the line: guided back, a new route, or just the direction back

Recording
 It keeps recording when the phone does not
 Recording runs in the background with a foreground notification on Android and a live activity on iOS, and survives the app being killed. Battery saver dims the screen and coarsens the GPS. Heart rate, cadence and power come along from an Apple Watch, a Bluetooth sensor or your health app, if you switch them on. Afterwards, ride pages with elevation, speed, heart rate, splits sized to the ride, the climbs you rode, the surface under your wheels from the offline map, and a speed-coloured track; on request calories, heart-rate and power zones, normalised power and an estimated power for rides without a meter.
 Background recording that survives the app being killed 
 Heart rate, cadence and power from a watch or a Bluetooth sensor, all optional 
 Ride pages with splits, climbs, surface and a speed-coloured track; calories, zones and estimated power if you want them 
Sensors
 Sensors and your watch
 Heart rate, cadence and power come from a Bluetooth sensor — a strap, a speed and cadence sensor or a power meter — paired once and then part of every ride: on the record screen while you ride, and kept with the ride afterwards. The Velorki app on your Apple Watch shows the ride on your wrist and sends your heart rate to the phone; start, pause and finish from the watch, and it keeps measuring through your stops, or rests at every stop if you prefer. Files and services
 Your rides are files you own
 GPX, FIT and TCX import and export through the share sheet and open-with, so routes and rides move to Komoot, Garmin Connect, Strava or anything else that reads those formats. A GPX route keeps its cue sheet and points of interest, and a Ride with GPS link opens in Velorki. Velorki works with Strava and Ride with GPS for free; share links are part of Plus. One Share button on a route or a ride holds the link, Strava and Ride with GPS.
 GPX, FIT and TCX in and out, from Files, Mail or a browser, with cue sheets and points of interest 
 A library of saved routes and recorded rides 
 Compatible with Strava and Ride with GPS, free; share links with Plus 
Cycle map
 The cycle map
 Bike lanes, cycle routes and one-way arrows drawn over the map from the data you already downloaded for routing. It works with no connection at all and shows up as you zoom in.
 What it draws
 Bike lanes & tracks
 Shared paths
 Two-way for bikes
 One-way arrows
 One-way streets
 National routes
 Regional routes
 Local routes
 Unpaved & bumpy
 Barriers & steps
 Calm streets
 Mountain bike
 Climbs
 Each part switches on and off on its own, in the map's Layers sheet. The chips there are the legend: each one shows its line.
 Stops on the map
 Cafés, drinking water, bakeries, toilets and repair stations to start with, from the same downloaded data. Pick any other kind from these groups, and tap a stop to plan to it. Zoomed out, close stops gather into bubbles with a count; single stops show from zoom 15, and along a route you see the stops ahead.
 Cycling stops
 Overnight
 Landmarks
Online cycle map
 CyclOSM's map is the alternative when you have a signal: it adds bike shops and parking, and needs a connection.
Offline from your downloaded areas: no extra download, no server. 
 How the map layers work 
Velorki Plus
 Ask for the ride you want
 Plus is the optional subscription for what needs our servers. Most of it is the assistant: you say what you have in mind, and the route is still planned on your phone.
 Describe a ride
 “A gravel loop of about 80 km on quiet roads” becomes a request the planner understands: a distance, a shape, places to pass. The route itself is planned on your phone.
Ask about the route on the map
 Have the route checked, find coffee around halfway or a tap to refill. Each finding has its place on the map, and Add as stop or Avoid changes the route in one step that Undo takes back.
A description for your routes
 Describe this route writes a paragraph from what the phone knows about the route: its climbs, surfaces, towns and the cafés along it.
Share links
 Share a route or a ride as a link that opens in any browser, with the map, the stats and a GPX download.
Finer weather along the route
 The free weather along the route comes from a coarser public forecast. Plus asks local weather services instead — the US National Weather Service, the Deutscher Wetterdienst's station forecasts in Germany, MET Norway elsewhere — for finer wind, rain and temperature, with gusts and the chance of rain.
Rain radar across Europe
 Where the free map has only satellite estimates, such as in France, Spain, Italy, the UK, Switzerland and Scandinavia, Plus shows real radar from EUMETNET OPERA and Radar-DPC (Italy): 1 km cells, a new image every 5 minutes, the last 2 hours.
The assistant asks before it sends anything: what you type and, only if you allow it, your position rounded to about a kilometre. No account, no route history.
 Monthly or yearly through the App Store or Google Play, with a free trial. The Plus page lists the price in your country.
 What Plus includes → How the assistant works → 
Free vs Plus
 Free is everything that runs on the phone
 Velorki Plus is a small subscription only for the parts that need our servers. Everything else is free, for everyone, for good.
 Free is everything that runs on the phone Feature Free Plus 
 Route planning, five bike profiles, alternatives Included Included 
 Elevation profile and surface statistics Included Included 
 Loops and round trips Included Included 
 Offline map and routing regions Included Included 
 Offline place and POI search Included Included

 Compatible with Strava: upload rides, import your routes Included Included 
 Compatible with Ride with GPS: routes and trips both ways Included Included 
 Finer weather along the route from local weather services, with gusts and chance of rain Not included Included 
 Real rain radar across Europe where the free map has only satellite estimates Not included Included 
 The assistant: a sentence becomes a route Not included Included 
 Share links for routes and rides Not included Included 
The code for all of it is here, so you can also run your own relay and skip the subscription entirely.
 Velorki Plus → 
Private, and anyone can check
 Everything runs on your phone and there is no account. Your routes and rides stay with you, or in your own iCloud or Google Drive, and leave as GPX, FIT or TCX whenever you like. The code is public, so anyone can check that and improve it: the app, the relay and this website are open source under the AGPL. Everything it draws, routes on and searches in comes from OpenStreetMap, the map anyone can edit.
 Read the source on GitHub Credits and licences 
In the browser
 Plan on a big screen
 The planner also runs in the browser: free, nothing to install, no account. It computes routes on your computer with the same routing as the app, from the routing data for the area you plan in.
 What it does
 Routes with the Touring, Road, Gravel and MTB profiles, variants and loops 
 Distance, ascent and the elevation profile, coloured by gradient or surface 
 Place search, the cycle map, stops along the way and the weather map 
 A library of your routes and rides, synced through your own iCloud or Google Drive, and GPX files to download 
What stays in the app
 Recording rides and turn-by-turn navigation 
 Map areas kept for riding without a signal 
 Strava and Ride with GPS 
The app is for riding: it records, navigates and works offline on the way.
 Open the planner Get the app 
 Velorki Plus is bought in the iPhone and Android apps; signed in to the iCloud or Google account the app syncs with, it works in the browser too. Get the app 
Questions
 Frequently asked
 Do I need an account?
 + No. There is no account and no sign-up, not even for Velorki Plus — a subscription is restored through the store you bought it in, without an account with us. Sync, if you want it, goes through your own iCloud or Google account.
 Does it really work without a connection?
 + Yes. Download a region once and the map, the routing, the place search and the spoken turns all run on the phone. Only the weather, the assistant, sync, the Strava and Ride with GPS connections and share links need a network.
 What does Velorki cost?
 + Everything that runs on the phone is free: planning, loops, offline maps and routing, search, navigation, recording, heart rate, cadence and power from your sensors, ride stats, the weather map, the weather along the route from a public forecast, GPX, FIT and TCX files, sync through your own iCloud or Google Drive, and the Strava and Ride with GPS connections. Velorki Plus is a subscription for the server-side features; the Plus page lists its monthly and yearly price per country, as the App Store and Google Play show them.
 What is Velorki Plus?
 + A small subscription for the parts that need our servers: the assistant, share links, finer weather along the route from local weather services and rain radar across Europe. It is bought, managed and cancelled in the App Store or Google Play.
 What leaves my phone?
 + Nothing, unless you ask for it. Routes, rides and settings are stored on the device; when you sync them, they go to your own iCloud or Google Drive, never to us. The assistant asks for consent before any text leaves, and rounds the position it sends to about a kilometre. Map tiles and online search are fetched only when you are not using downloaded data.
 Where does the map data come from?
 + From OpenStreetMap, under the ODbL. The map, the routing and the place search all run on that open data; the projects and licences behind it are on the credits page.
 Credits and licences 
 Is Velorki really open source?
 + Yes, so anyone can check what it does with your data. The app, its pure-Dart packages, the relay and this website are AGPL-3.0-only; all of it is on GitHub. The name, logo and icon are reserved, so a fork has to rebrand before publishing it to a store.
 Can I run the server parts myself?
 + Yes. The relay, a routing server and a tile host can all be self-hosted; the repository has the compose files and the systemd units. A fork that points at its own relay needs no subscription at all.
Get the app and ride
 Free on both stores. No account, no ads, no trial on the parts that run on your phone, and the source is on GitHub for anyone to check.

title: Show HN: My first project, an AI-powered financial news analyzer
author: lamarcol
body: I'm 17, and I started NotBot a few months ago to see whether I could turn an idea into a working project. My main interest is economics, not becoming a programmer, but I enjoy experimenting with code.A few months ago, I had the idea of creating a program that would analyze the most recent news about a specific stock and calculate a weighted average of their polarity to create a sort of sentiment indicator.While researching, I found a YouTube video about creating a simple GitHub repository that did, in a simplified and imprecise way, what I had in mind. At first glance, I realized it was a very simple program: feedparser retrieved news from Google News, beautifulsoup4 extracted the content, the sentiment was analyzed with FinBERT, running through Transformers and PyTorch.From there, I started modifying it with the free versions of Gemini. I had to solve a lot of problems, for example fixing the extraction of articles from Google News, I managed to solve it with a new library (googlenewsdecoder).Then I had to replace FinBERT, because it classified sentiment based on the context of the words but didn't take into account the actual impact of the event using external sources.I experimented with an LLM that allowed me to specify the evaluation criteria more precisely through a prompt. I found a free one with rather strict TPM and RPM limits (it was called openai/gpt-oss-120b).I also created two coefficients: one that adjusted the reliability of the news based on its source, and another that adjusted its impact based on how recent it was (all selected news articles had been published within the last 24 hours). Each article was divided into title, description, and content, and each of these three sections had a different weight based on predefined values (title 35%, description 25%, and text 40%). If the content had fewer than 100 characters, the text was not assigned any weight, and the title accounted for 60% while the description accounted for 40%.After these modifications, I took a break of about a month because of school commitments, during which I discovered Codex (OpenAI's agent).I changed the main LLM and implemented Gemini (3.1 Flash-Lite) because the TPM limits of the LLM I was using were too restrictive.Even though I started using Gemini, I didn't discard Groq. In fact, I used it as a fallback in case Gemini returned some kind of error.Another important modification was the addition of asynchronous article downloading through aiohttp and the processing of multiple articles simultaneously through asyncio. Later, I decided to start using Groq again for article analysis. In fact, I had both LLMs analyze the longer articles and then calculated the average of their two polarity scores.The first was Finnhub, which allowed me to search for many more news articles about a specific stock (by entering its name and ticker).At that point, I had to split up the code because the script had become very long.The last modification I made concerned news selection: I implemented a filter that prevented similar news articles from being selected, to avoid excessively distorting the polarity in an incorrect way.First of all, I'd like to know, from an expert, how well the project is built from a structural point of view and how it could be improved. For future projects, what parameters should I take into consideration to understand whether a project is well built?Secondly, I'd like to know how I can determine whether a program like this can actually work, or at least how it could be useful (even with some modifications).The third and final point is: which aspects of the pipeline might require more attention or could be optimized? Does it make sense to continue working on the project (also with the idea of turning it into a product), or am I approaching a structural limit?

title: Show HN: Record, branch, and compare command runs in stdlib-only Python
author: protention
body: Hi, this is a package I developed for keeping track of short toy-model development cycles and explaining what changed between runs.The core idea: commands run through the package, and their declared parameters (or injected parameters with --substitute) and outcomes go into a dependency-free ledger stored in the project. Because that ledger lives in the project directory, it has worked well for passing context between different agents. I’ve also found some use for it in CI work.

title: Show HN: SafeScript, a safe version of JavaScript for executing untrusted code
author: EGreg

comments.author: Rohansi
comments.text: What's stopping malicious scripts from sucking up the host's memory?

comments.author: ranger_danger
comments.text: I think they're using a slightly different definition of "safe" than you are

comments.author: EGreg
EGreg
comments.text: It’s not the job of a language to solve everything. Sometimes the solution belongs in sandboxing and virtual machines. You should be isolating untrusted code anyway.SafeScript was just inspired by Google’s CaJa project from 10 years ago. My Qbix Webserver started rewriting PHP before loading it, and I wondered what if I could start over and just reduce the language the way JSON reduced it to just data, and was wildly successful. I chose JS as the base because it’s everywhere. I then made it also execute inside PHP. I made it auto-await every promise so it could work in non-evented environments like vanilla PHP.This could be the next Lua, for instance, but for the modern era and far safer.Having said that… there may be some static analysis you could do, to conservatively overestimate how much memory any given program could waste, and reject those that COULD waste it. The nice thing about static analysis is you only have to run it once per particular script.

# Bulk-harden your GitHub repo settings

- Owner: 1ch4k
- Created: 2026-11-08T20:23:03Z
- Public: yes
- Comments: 0
- Forks: 0

## harden_github_repos.py

Language: Python

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["playwright"]
# ///
"""
harden_github_repos.py: bulk-harden the settings of every public repo you own on GitHub.

For each repo it opens the settings in a real browser window and:
 * Features -> turns the Wiki off (or only restricts editing, see --wiki)
 * Advanced Security -> enables Private vulnerability reporting,
 Secret Protection and Push protection
Steps that are already done are skipped, so it is safe to re-run after creating new repos.

Why a browser and not the API? It needs no token at all: you sign in to GitHub yourself
in the window that opens, and the script only clicks the same buttons you would.

Usage (needs uv: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):
 uv run harden_github_repos.py --dry-run # show what would change, click nothing
 uv run harden_github_repos.py # apply
Options:
 --owner NAME account to process (default: the account you sign in with)
 --wiki restrict keep wikis but only collaborators can edit (default: off)
 --no-pvr don't touch Private vulnerability reporting
 --skip a,b repo names to leave alone
 --browser PATH Chromium-based browser to drive (default: Brave/Chrome/Edge if
 installed, else Playwright's own Chromium)
 --debug save the HTML of pages where a step was skipped (they contain
 session tokens: don't share them)

Notes:
 * Only public, non-archived repos are listed (via the public API, no auth).
 * The browser uses its own profile (~/.cache/harden-github-repos), never your everyday one;
 browsers refuse automation on the default profile. Delete that folder when you're done
 so no signed-in session is left behind.
 * GitHub changes its UI from time to time. If a step says "skipped", check it by hand.
"""
import argparse
import json
import shutil
import sys
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, TimeoutError as PWTimeout

PROFILE = Path.home() / ".cache" / "harden-github-repos"
DEBUG_DIR = Path.cwd() / "gh-debug"
BROWSER_CANDIDATES = [
 r"C:\Program Files\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\Application\brave.exe",
 r"C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe",
 r"C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe",
 "/Applications/Brave Browser.app/Contents/MacOS/Brave Browser",
 "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome",
 "brave", "brave-browser", "google-chrome", "chromium", "microsoft-edge",
]

args = None

def parse_args():
 p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Bulk-harden your GitHub repo settings via the web UI.")
 p.add_argument("--owner")
 p.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")
 p.add_argument("--wiki", choices=["off", "restrict"], default="off")
 p.add_argument("--no-pvr", action="store_true")
 p.add_argument("--skip", default="")
 p.add_argument("--browser")
 p.add_argument("--debug", action="store_true")
 return p.parse_args()

def find_browser():
 if args.browser:
 return args.browser
 for c in BROWSER_CANDIDATES:
 if Path(c).is_file():
 return c
 found = shutil.which(c)
 if found:
 return found
 return None # Playwright's bundled Chromium

def list_repos(owner):
 url = f"https://api.github.com/users/{owner}/repos?per_page=100&type=owner"
 with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=20) as r:
 repos = json.load(r)
 skip = {s.strip() for s in args.skip.split(",") if s.strip()}
 return [x["name"] for x in repos if not x["archived"] and x["name"] not in skip]

def log(repo, msg):
 print(f" [{repo}] {msg}")

def settle(page):
 # GitHub keeps a websocket open, so "networkidle" never fires; wait for the DOM + a moment.
 try:
 page.wait_for_load_state("domcontentloaded", timeout=15000)
 except PWTimeout:
 pass
 page.wait_for_timeout(1500)

def goto(page, url):
 page.goto(url, wait_until="domcontentloaded", timeout=45000)
 settle(page)

def dump(page, repo, step):
 if not args.debug:
 return
 try:
 DEBUG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
 f = DEBUG_DIR / f"{repo}-{step}.html"
 f.write_text(page.content(), encoding="utf-8")
 log(repo, f"(saved page to {f})")
 except Exception as e:
 log(repo, f"(could not save debug page: {e})")

def ensure_login(page):
 """Wait until signed in (GitHub sets logged_in=yes), then return the signed-in username."""
 def logged_in():
 return any(c["name"] == "logged_in" and c["value"] == "yes"
 for c in page.context.cookies("https://github.com"))
 if not logged_in():
 goto(page, "https://github.com/login")
 print("\n>>> Sign in to GitHub in the browser window (incl. 2FA). Waiting...")
 while not logged_in():
 page.wait_for_timeout(2000)
 print(">>> Signed in.\n")
 goto(page, "https://github.com/")
 meta = page.locator('meta[name="user-login"]')
 return meta.first.get_attribute("content") if meta.count() else None

def set_checkbox(page, repo, label, want, selector):
 # Select by id: get_by_label("Wikis") also matches a.
 box = page.locator(selector)
 if box.count() == 0:
 log(repo, f"'{label}' not found (skipped)")
 dump(page, repo, label.replace(" ", "_"))
 return
 box = box.first
 state = "on" if want else "off"
 if box.is_checked() == want:
 log(repo, f"'{label}' already {state}")
 return
 if args.dry_run:
 log(repo, f"would turn '{label}' {state}")
 return
 box.click()
 settle(page)
 log(repo, f"'{label}' -> {state}")

def fix_features(page, owner, repo):
 goto(page, f"https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/settings")
 if "/settings" not in page.url:
 log(repo, "no access to settings (not yours?)")
 return
 if args.wiki == "off":
 set_checkbox(page, repo, "Wikis", False, "input#wiki-feature")
 else:
 set_checkbox(page, repo, "Wikis", True, "input#wiki-feature")
 set_checkbox(page, repo, "Restrict editing to collaborators only", True, "input#wiki-pusher-access")

def section(page, title):
 """The smallest block around `title` (heading or plain text) that contains a button."""
 return page.get_by_text(title, exact=True).first.locator("xpath=ancestor::*[.//button][1]")

def confirm_dialog(page):
 dlg = page.locator('[role="dialog"]:visible, dialog[open]')
 try:
 dlg.first.wait_for(timeout=2500)
 except PWTimeout:
 return
 btn = dlg.first.get_by_role("button", name="Enable").or_(
 dlg.first.get_by_role("button", name="Confirm")).first
 if btn.count():
 btn.click()
 settle(page)

def click_enable(page, repo, title):
 """Returns True if the feature is (now) enabled."""
 if page.get_by_text(title, exact=True).count() == 0:
 log(repo, f"'{title}' not on page (skipped)")
 dump(page, repo, title.replace(" ", "_"))
 return False
 enable = section(page, title).get_by_role("button", name="Enable", exact=True)
 if enable.count() == 0:
 log(repo, f"{title} already enabled")
 return True
 if args.dry_run:
 log(repo, f"would enable {title}")
 return False
 enable.first.click()
 confirm_dialog(page)
 settle(page)
 log(repo, f"{title} -> enabled")
 return True

def flip_toggle(page, repo, label, depends_on_previous=False):
 row = page.locator("div, li").filter(has_text=label).filter(
 has=page.locator("button[aria-pressed]")).last
 if row.count() == 0:
 if depends_on_previous:
 log(repo, f"{label} appears once Secret Protection is on (applied in the real run)")
 else:
 log(repo, f"'{label}' toggle not found (skipped)")
 dump(page, repo, label.replace(" ", "_"))
 return
 toggle = row.locator("button[aria-pressed]").first
 if toggle.get_attribute("aria-pressed") == "true":
 log(repo, f"{label} already on")
 return
 if args.dry_run:
 log(repo, f"would turn {label} on")
 return
 toggle.click()
 confirm_dialog(page)
 settle(page)
 log(repo, f"{label} -> on")

def fix_security(page, owner, repo):
 url = f"https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/settings/security_analysis"
 goto(page, url)
 if not args.no_pvr:
 click_enable(page, repo, "Private vulnerability reporting")
 sp_on = click_enable(page, repo, "Secret Protection")
 goto(page, url) # fresh page so the Push protection toggle shows up
 flip_toggle(page, repo, "Push protection", depends_on_previous=not sp_on)

def main():
 global args
 args = parse_args()
 browser = find_browser()
 print("Browser:", browser or "Playwright's Chromium")
 with sync_playwright() as pw:
 opts = dict(headless=False, viewport=None, chromium_sandbox=True)
 if browser:
 opts["executable_path"] = browser
 try:
 ctx = pw.chromium.launch_persistent_context(str(PROFILE), **opts)
 except Exception:
 if browser:
 raise
 sys.exit("No browser found. Pass --browser PATH, or run: uv run --with playwright playwright install chromium")
 page = ctx.pages[0] if ctx.pages else ctx.new_page()
 me = ensure_login(page)
 owner = args.owner or me
 if not owner:
 sys.exit("Couldn't detect your username; pass --owner NAME.")
 repos = list_repos(owner)
 print(f"{owner}: {len(repos)} public repos")
 failed = []
 for repo in repos:
 print(f"\n== {repo}")
 try:
 fix_features(page, owner, repo)
 fix_security(page, owner, repo)
 except Exception as e: # keep going with the next repo
 log(repo, f"ERROR: {str(e).splitlines()[0]}")
 failed.append(repo)
 print("\nDone." + (f" Check these by hand: {', '.join(failed)}" if failed else ""))
 if args.dry_run:
 print("(dry run: nothing was changed)")
 print(f"Tip: delete {PROFILE} when finished so no signed-in session is left behind.")
 input("Press Enter to close the browser...")
 ctx.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
 main()


# alam00000/bentopdf-hyper-compress

title: Show HN: Hyper Compress: The Best Open Source PDF Compression Engine
author: __alam__
body:
# alam00000/bentopdf-hyper-compress

Best Open Source PDF Compression Engine

- Stars: 9
- Forks: 1
- Watchers: 9
- Open issues: 1
- License: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
- Homepage: hyper.bentopdf.com
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-08-25T09:12:33Z

## Languages

- C
- C++
- CSS
- Dockerfile
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Makefile
- Python
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Topics

- compression
- compression-library
- docker
- jbig2
- jpegli
- nodejs
- pdf
- pdf-compress
- pdf-compression
- pdf-compressor
- pdfium
- self-hosted
- self-hosting
- wasm

## Top Contributors

- alam00000 (1 contributions)

---

## README

 

 Hyper Compress 

 
 The best open source PDF compression engine. 
 

Hyper Compress is a high fidelity, content preserving PDF compression engine built to make PDFs smaller without unnecessarily changing the document.

Hyper Compress is built by the BentoPDF team. The same engine is available as a CLI, Node SDK, C library, self hosted service, and a WebAssembly build that runs entirely in the browser.

Try it at hyper.bentopdf.com. Full documentation lives at hyper.bentopdf.com/docs.

License: AGPL v3 GitHub Stars

---

## Table of Contents

* Why Hyper Compress
* Benchmarks
* Install
* Usage

 * CLI
 * Node SDK
 * Self-hosted service
 * Browser (WebAssembly)
 * C API
* Compression Levels
* What the Engine Does
* What the Engine Refuses to Do
* Building from Source
* Testing
* Project Layout
* Licensing
* Contributing

---

## Why Hyper Compress

PDF compression has three major problems: **files ending up being larger after compression, sacrificing document content for size, and producing PDFs that are broken and non conforming.**

Hyper Compress is built around solving these three problems.

* **Monotonic compression.** Hyper never returns a larger file. If compression does not save space, the original PDF is returned unchanged. 

* **Content preserving compression.** Hyper includes a true lossless mode for compression without image re encoding or quality loss. For more aggressive compression, it preserves searchable text and document structure while making only the changes required by the selected compression level all while producing a conforming PDF.

* **Built for reliability.** Hyper validates its output and verifies transformations that can affect visual fidelity. When a change cannot reproduce a page faithfully, it is rolled back. Across the benchmark, Hyper had a **0.39% corruption rate**, the lowest of any engine measured.

* **One engine, everywhere.** The same compression engine powers the CLI, Node SDK, C API, self-hosted service, and WebAssembly build.

---

## Benchmarks

Hyper Compress was benchmarked against Ghostscript, MuPDF, and qpdf using **2,104 real world PDFs from four public corpora**, for a total of **27,352 engine runs**.

Visual fidelity was measured with Poppler, which was deliberately chosen as an independent renderer rather than one shared by the engines being tested.

The full methodology, per-file results, and complete document list are available in comparison.md.

Median size reduction at the median worst page SSIM:

| Tier | Hyper | Ghostscript | MuPDF | qpdf |
| -------- | ----------------- | ------------- | ------------- | ------------ |
| Lossless | **22.4% @ 1.000** | 21.1% @ 0.997 | 4.7% @ 1.000 | 6.3% @ 1.000 |
| 300 dpi | **52.3% @ 1.000** | 19.1% @ 0.996 | 14.0% @ 1.000 | n/a |
| 150 dpi | **58.2% @ 0.999** | 42.4% @ 0.994 | 19.4% @ 1.000 | n/a |
| 72 dpi | **64.8% @ 0.996** | 53.9% @ 0.990 | 28.0% @ 0.999 | n/a |

Robustness across the same benchmark:

| Engine | Runs | Corrupt | Grew the file |
| ----------- | ----: | -------------: | ------------: |
| **Hyper** | 8,416 | **33 (0.39%)** | **0** |
| qpdf | 2,104 | 1 (0.05%) | 53 (2.5%) |
| Ghostscript | 8,416 | 256 (3.04%) | 2,089 (24.8%) |
| MuPDF | 8,416 | 333 (3.96%) | 70 (0.8%) |

> [!NOTE]
> The corpus selection was pre registered using a fixed seed before any files were fetched. Every document's SHA-256 hash and origin URL are recorded, so the benchmark can be independently reproduced.
>
> You can also run the harness against your own documents:
>
> `make bench CORPUS=path/to/corpus`

---

## Install

Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux, and Windows are attached to each release.

Download the archive for your platform, verify it against `SHA256SUMS`, and unpack it into `cli/prebuilt/`.

For the self-hosted service:

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/alam00000/bentopdf-hyper-compress:latest
```

To build the engine yourself, see BUILDING.md.

---

## Usage

### CLI

```bash
hyper input.pdf                                     # writes input-compressed.pdf

hyper input.pdf output.pdf                          # medium preset (default)

hyper input.pdf output.pdf --preset high            # smallest output

hyper scan.pdf out.pdf --target-size 2MB            # specify a target size

hyper locked.pdf out.pdf --password hunter2         # encrypted input

hyper in.pdf out.pdf --set grayscale=true           # override an option

hyper --help                                        # every flag, with examples
```

`--target-size` searches for the highest image quality that fits under your target, pushing down to quality 5 and 36 dpi if it has to. If the target is reachable you get the best looking file that fits; if it is not, you get the smallest file the engine could produce along with a warning saying how small that was.

### Node SDK

```js
import { compress } from 'hyper-compress';

const r = await compress({
  sourcePath: 'input.pdf',
  savePath: 'output.pdf',
  preset: 'medium',
});

console.log(r.originalSize, '->', r.compressedSize);
```

The result includes the original and compressed sizes, whether the document was signed, its declared PDF/A level, and whether a requested target size was reached.

Errors are typed:

`decrypt_failed`, `engine_error`, `timeout`, `cancelled`.

Parsing runs in a worker subprocess with a timeout. If hostile or malformed input causes the worker to fail, it is isolated from your main process.

### Self-hosted service

The Docker image includes a web interface at `http://localhost:8080` and an HTTP API.

Your files are processed on your own server.

```bash
curl -o out.pdf --data-binary @in.pdf \
  'http://localhost:8080/api/compress?preset=high'
```

See SELF-HOSTING.md for the complete API, configuration options, and deployment notes.

### Browser (WebAssembly)

The `web/` directory contains a complete browser build.

The engine is compiled to WebAssembly and runs locally in the browser. Files are not uploaded, and the build makes is air gapped by default.

The same WebAssembly build is on npm as `hyper-compress-wasm`, a buffer-based SDK for platforms the native package does not cover:

```js
import { compress } from 'hyper-compress-wasm';

const result = await compress(pdfBytes, { preset: 'medium' });
```

```bash
node wasm/verify.mjs some.pdf
```

This verifies that the WebAssembly output is byte-identical to the native build.

### C API

`sdk/native` exposes a small C ABI:

* `hpdf_compress_file`
* `hpdf_compress_buffer`
* `hpdf_last_error`

The shared library exports only these symbols, and the ABI is additive only within a major version.

---

## Compression Levels

| Preset | Image quality | Max DPI | Use for |
| ---------- | ------------: | ------: | ------------------------------------------ |
| `low` | 80 | 200 | Archival copies and minimal visible change |
| `medium` | 50 | 150 | The default; good for sharing and email |
| `high` | 20 | 72 | Smallest output and screen reading |
| `lossless` | n/a | none | No image re-encoding; pixel-identical |

Every option behind these presets is also available individually.

You can create custom profiles using image quality and resolution, grayscale conversion, colour reduction, font subsetting and unembedding, metadata and annotation stripping, PDF 2.0 Brotli streams, and page rasterisation for image-only documents.

---

## What the Engine Does

Depending on the document and selected options, the engine can:

* re encode images with jpegli
* downsample images above a configured resolution ceiling
* choose between JPEG, JPEG 2000, Flate, CCITT, and JBIG2 on a per image basis
* convert Type 1 fonts to CFF
* subset embedded fonts to the glyphs actually used
* merge duplicate font programs
* unembed fonts that are metric-compatible clones of the standard 14 fonts
* regenerate content streams with correct handling for CMYK, CalRGB, Lab, ICCBased, Separation, DeviceN, Indexed, and pattern fills
* deduplicate identical objects and prune unused resources
* flatten ICC profiles
* remove selected metadata
* optionally apply PDF 2.0 Brotli stream compression
* optionally rasterise pages when the document is genuinely image-only

The engine applies multiple techniques mentioned above to achieve best possible compression.

---

## Building from Source

The JavaScript parts require Node 22:

```bash
npm ci

make check
```

The native engine builds against a pinned PDFium checkout. The initial bootstrap is several gigabytes.

See BUILDING.md for complete instructions, the patch inventory, and platform-specific notes.

---

## Testing

```bash
make check                      # typecheck, lint, unit and integration tests

make regress                    # regression failset, every preset

make bench CORPUS=path/to/dir   # benchmark harness from comparison.md

make fuzz                       # libFuzzer harness
```

`make regress` is the gate for bug fixes.

Every PDF in `tests/regression/failset/` represents a file that previously exposed a bug. The suite checks validity, pixel fidelity, and text-layer survival across every relevant preset.

A clean run reports zero failing pairs.

Fuzzing runs through ClusterFuzzLite on every pull request that touches the engine, and again nightly for a longer session. Discovered crashes are pinned as regression seeds.

---

## Licensing

Hyper Compress is licensed under the GNU AGPL v3.

If you need to use Hyper Compress in a proprietary or closed-source product, a commercial license is available. Contact us at contact@bentopdf.com.

Bundled third-party components retain their own licenses. See NOTICE.md for the full list.

---

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome.

Before opening your first pull request, there are two things to know:

1. Contributors need to sign the Contributor License Agreement. The bot will prompt you automatically.
2. Bug fixes should include the PDF that reproduces the issue so it can be added to the regression suite.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for the full contribution guide.

For security vulnerabilities, please see SECURITY.md.

title: Show HN: A medieval world where growth and citizens are pure functions of time
author: doener
body:
# retrogames23/samenland

A cozy, historically grounded real-time medieval settlement simulation set in Northern Germany around 1500. Pure deterministic growth, isometric 2:1 canvas engine.

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: Other
- Homepage: https://samenland.app/
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-06T20:42:12Z

## Languages

- CSS
- JavaScript
- PLpgSQL
- TypeScript

## Top Contributors

- lovable-dev[bot] (2776 contributions)

---

## README

# Samenland

**A slow, cozy, shared settlement game set in Northern Germany around 1500.**

Plant a single seed somewhere on a large shared map — and watch a hamlet grow, in real time, into a village, a market town and eventually a Hanseatic city. Your town keeps growing whether you are watching or not. Every now and then you step in: you decide on trade roads, answer visitors, commission buildings and walk through the streets as the village mayor (*Schulze*).

Live: **https://samenland.app**

## Features

- **Real-time, deterministic growth** – towns are a pure function of their seed position and founding time, so every player sees exactly the same town, even offline.
- **Shared multiplayer maps** – four regional realms, each with its own clock; neighbouring towns connect by trade roads and slowly grow together.
- **Living villagers** – every resident has a home, a craft, a daily routine, Sundays, weddings, illness and feasts, all derived from the shared clock.
- **Historical setting** – Northern Germany c. 1500: church feasts, three-field rotation, guilds, the prince's court, fires, floods and raids.
- **Day, night, seasons and weather** – real sunrise/sunset times per realm, seasonal art and atmospheric weather.
- **Isometric painted look** – 2:1 isometric canvas renderer with sprites, night window layers and depth-sorted occlusion.
- **Eight languages** – German, English, French, Spanish, Arabic (RTL), Hindi, Simplified Chinese and Japanese.

## Tech stack

- TanStack Start (React 19, SSR, server functions) on Vite 7
- TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4
- HTML5 Canvas renderer (no game engine)
- Supabase-compatible backend (Postgres, auth, realtime) via Lovable Cloud
- Vitest for tests

## Getting started

Requirements: Node.js 20+ (or Bun).

```sh
git clone <this-repository-url>
cd samenland
npm install        # or: bun install
npm run dev        # starts the dev server on http://localhost:8080
npm test           # runs the test suite
```

The app expects backend credentials in `.env` (`VITE_SUPABASE_URL`, `VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`, `VITE_SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID`). Database migrations live in `supabase/migrations/`.

## Project structure

```text
src/
  game/         simulation, economy, villagers, seasons, weather and the canvas renderer
    lang/       game texts and translation catalogs
  components/   React UI (HUD, windows, overlays)
  routes/       TanStack routes and server endpoints
  assets/       sprites, music and sound
supabase/       database migrations and configuration
```

Design rules for each area are documented in the `AGENTS.md` files throughout the repository — please read them before changing game logic. The key principle: **game state is derived, not stored.** Growth, villagers, goods and events are computed from seeds and the shared clock; the database stores only player decisions.

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome — see CONTRIBUTING.md.

title: Show HN: Nexjoin – A C++ remote desktop alternative (Windows XP+, macOS 10.13)
author: szigand
body:
Rethinking Remote Desktop 
 The Engine and Platforms 
Display and Control

Security, Personal Data, Privacy 
Current State 
Source Code Audit
