Blog | LinkedIn | Contact | Download    [ English | Hungarian ]
Rethinking Remote Desktop 
 Many years ago, as a former LogMeIn developer, starting my own remote desktop system from scratch seemed like an interesting idea and a good challenge, especially since there were more and more complaints about the existing ones. I saw no point in developing yet another identical system, but rethinking what I could, putting in new ideas, and polishing every detail with proper implementation - while respecting future users' time, nerves, and private data - seemed like a good task. It should just do its job simply, cleanly, and unnoticed as it should: removing distance, making remote work easier and a better experience, and simplifying connections while taking care of security. For now, this is what came out of it. This is just a first incarnation of the engine; many kinds of products can be born from this. 
 Try it out, and if you like this direction, let's keep it alive together! 
 The Engine and Platforms 
 Modular, multi-platform, native C++ engine for developing all kinds of remote desktop software 
x86, x64, ARM, Apple Silicon 
Windows XP SP3/Vista/7/8/8.1/10/11 and their server versions 
From macOS 10.13 (not tested on macOS 27 yet) 
Linux and Windows ARM32/64 are planned 
~300,000 lines, ~1,400 source files of custom code 
Display and Control 
 Per-window control: when you don't need the entire remote desktop 
 Run any number of windows from one or more remote machines as if they were running directly on your local desktop 
Resize windows locally 
Use the remote macOS menu bar, displayed right above the local window 
Pop-up windows extending beyond the main window are also rendered and properly clipped 
Keyboard handling: 
 Unicode: Type using your local keyboard layout, even if it is not installed on the remote machine 
Physical: Use the remote layout if it fits better, or if the remote application does not handle Unicode characters properly 
Switch between local and remote input languages locally 
Clipboard management: 
 Beyond plain text, supports multiple formats (rich text, HTML, images, vector graphics, audio) as permitted between the respective operating systems 
Synchronizes large clipboard contents, even many megabytes in size 
Copy and paste multiple gigabytes of files - including subdirectories - directly between file managers across different operating systems (between local and remote, or even between multiple remote machines) 
Monitors bandwidth and the other machine's CPU load during transfers, preventing the system from becoming unresponsive when handling large payloads 
Mouse handling: Server-side mouse cursor movement takes priority 
Multi-monitor handling 
Retina resolution support, with the option to turn it off 
Remote screen blanking on supported operating systems (Windows 10/11, macOS) 
Accessing Windows Terminal Session desktops: 
 no RDP client, firewall configuration, or VPN needed 
on Windows 8.1+, logging into a disconnected session (using the FreeRDP library through localhost) 
Parallel access to macOS Fast User Switching desktops if multiple users have logged-in desktops on one machine 
Screen locking (Windows 8.1+, macOS): switch to a virtual session while the remote machine's physical display returns to the login screen, hiding your activity. On Windows, you can freely toggle back and forth between the physical and virtual views. 
Desktop panic button: kicks all remote clients off the machine 
System and Network 
 Linux servers: 
 Minimal C++ code in a single binary for security and performance 
Non-blocking I/O socket handling (libevent) 
SQL database for the Login/Contact servers 
Peer-to-peer: 
 IPv4/IPv6 
UPnP, NAT-PMP, SIP ALG, H.323 ALG port opening on the router (can be disabled) 
UDP (QUIC) and TCP connections 
System Tray/Menu Bar menu: for practical, quick access to remote machines/desktops/windows 
Join Code sharing: sharing your own machine, desktop, or window with someone else using a 9-digit code 
Local network: optionally, you can turn on finding and accessing local machines without servers ( Settings->Network->Find Nexjoin devices on the local network, Settings->Sharing->Visible on local network ) 
Security, Personal Data, Privacy 
 Cryptography: 
 OpenSSL 3.5.9 LTS 
RSA-2048 TLS 1.3 peer-to-peer connections 
RSA-4096 based server certificates 
Ed25519 based client certificates 
Argon2 password-hash, recovery-code-hash 
AES-256-CTR Randomized IV client-side encryption 
Server-side zero-knowledge: 
 Login servers: 
 all personal data (password, name, profile icon, key) is encrypted on the client side, only the account name is unencrypted (minimum GDPR) 
they send clients on to the Contact servers with a signed UserId/DeviceId, without personal data 
Contact servers: 
 only work with UserId/DeviceId, they know nothing about the clients 
all personal data that remote desktop clients might need (machine name, OS version, icon, key, Join Code sharing) is encrypted on the client side (AES-256-CTR) 
Relay servers: 
 don't even know the UserId/DeviceId of the clients 
hand out ticket pairs at the request of Contact servers to pair up incoming clients at the start of a remote connection 
Replaceable Login servers: independent from Contact/Relay servers, later they can even be connected to local company systems (e.g. Active Directory, LDAP) 
Certificate verification: on both client and server sides, issuing temporary certificates when redirecting clients between servers. Completely closed system. 
End-to-end encryption: 
 TLS connection with the Relay server until client ticket check 
after pairing the clients, the Relay switches back to a plain socket, and the clients create a new TLS connection between each other over the forwarded connection, mutually checking each other's peer-to-peer certificate 
the Relay server cannot inspect the data stream either, it just forwards it 
in parallel with the live Relay server connection, clients also try to create a direct connection between each other, and switch to it if successful (this can be turned off) 
IPC encryption: communication between processes is also encrypted with TLS 1.3 
Transparency: data communication can be checked by turning on debug logging 
Saved remote passwords: double encryption, encrypted by both the remote machine and the client side with their own keys, cannot be decrypted on either side without the other 
Two-factor authentication: using Google Authenticator or other TOTP programs 
Forgotten Nexjoin password: Recovery Codes to get your account back 
Current State 
 This is closed-source code developed the classic way over many years, in early beta state, from a single developer. It is not completely finished, but what is done is already works well in practice right now. Minor inaccuracies can of course still happen. What is still planned: 
 Audio 
Localization to as many languages as possible 
Using TPM/Secure Enclave 
Two-factor authentication when accessing remote machines too 
Wake-on-Lan 
Convenient switching between multiple monitors 
Drawing on the remote screen (whiteboard) 
Proper Windows HDR color conversion 
Opening a new Windows Terminal Session 
DirectX 9 Screen Capture (Windows Vista & Windows 7 DWM) 
Hardware video encoding/decoding 
Handling proxies 
Remote Update 
Mobile/tablet clients 
Deployable servers for your own network 
Optional PTSD mode: unexpected cancellation of the Free license, occasional nagging with popup windows, unexpected connection drops, filling out repentant confessions (for temporary management of withdrawal symptoms) 
And whatever else comes... :) Even your ideas. 
Source Code Audit 
 So far I have done everything I can for security and privacy, but auditing the code with an outside expert is also planned. 
 Code Signing 
 The code is signed with my own name on both Windows and macOS (András Szigethy, https://www.linkedin.com/in/szigand/ ). On Windows, my Sectigo Individual Code Sign Certificate is still quite new, so Windows Defender SmartScreen might complain for a while on first start. You can step past that, and in theory it will calm down over time once enough people have done it. 
 On Windows Server 2003, update KB3072630 is required for signature verification; without it, the program will not start. 
 Support 
 If you like the idea, want this software to be completed and kept running, and would use and rely on it in production in the not-too-distant future, please support it on Patreon , or if you prefer not to register just for this - or are contributing as a company and need a B2B invoice - you can also do so on Polar . I cannot continue without support, and I do not want to get deeply involved in the business world. I also welcome sponsors, including for server infrastructure. This is an experiment to see whether this project can be viable and grow organically in this form, while preserving its independence and common sense. 
 Open Source 
 The code relies on several very good, freely usable open-source libraries (Poco C++, wxWidgets, SDL, etc.). My firm goal is that if the project gets on a stable footing, I will regularly send 10% of the incoming money to them, since without their persistent work this couldn't have been created either, and couldn't really exist in the future, so I think they deserve this. 
 Usage 
 The program can also be used in STANDALONE MODE as a client, without installation, to access remote or local machines. 
Sharing the screen requires installation because of the necessary system components needed to make remote access to desktops actually usable. 
If you want to access your own remote machines, you can register a Nexjoin account and assign your machines to it one by one after installation. 
You can assign icons to your machines ( .svg, .icns, .png, .gif, .jpg, .jpeg, .bmp, .tif, .tiff ), which are stored on the server after client-side encryption. You can even use a logo, emblem, or product photo copied straight from a website. ( macOS Windows XP/7 Windows Vista Windows 8/8.1/10 Windows 11 ) 
If you only want to occasionally share something from your machine with a Join Code, you don't need a Nexjoin account for that, but installation is required. 
You can also share your machines one by one with other users so they can access them anytime. They can log into the desktops of these machines either with the password of the given desktop user, or by knocking if the user sitting at the machine lets them in. You can revoke the sharing anytime. 
You can share a complete desktop, a whole screen, or even a currently open window with a Join Code, even remotely. 
Join Code sharing requires the machines to be connected online to the Nexjoin server. 
Changing machine names and icons requires the machines to be assigned to an account. 
Current Servers 
 Login/Contact servers (because of GDPR, currently): 
 Budapest (HU) 
Frankfurt (DE) 
Amsterdam (NL) 
Relay servers: 
 Budapest (HU) 
Frankfurt (DE) 
Beauharnois (CA) 
Hillsboro (US) 
Singapore (SG) 
Sydney (AU) 
The servers use the downloaded DBIP IP to City Lite database so they can direct clients to the closest servers if needed. 
 For now, there are only these few servers so the system can be tried out at all; live production use will obviously require more later. 
 Uninstallation 
 Windows: from the Control Panel, just like other programs. 
macOS: drag the icon to the Trash, the Launch Daemon notices this and deletes itself along with the Launch Agent. 
Contact 
 You can find the project blog at https://blog.nexjoin.io/ , where I post news and updates. You can also subscribe to the email newsletter there. 
My LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/szigand/ 
Project email addresses: 
 András Szigethy <andras.szigethy@nexjoin.io> 
admin@nexjoin.io 
support@nexjoin.io 
bugs@nexjoin.io 
security@nexjoin.io 
privacy@nexjoin.io

FAQ 01 What is Recto? Recto is a visual design canvas for coding agents. It lets you create UI, motion, SVG and 3D designs with agents such as Claude Code and Codex while keeping everything directly editable. 02 Is Recto an AI model? No. Recto works with the coding agents already installed on your computer instead of replacing them. 03 Which coding agents does Recto support? Recto automatically detects supported coding agents installed on your system and lets you use them directly inside Recto. You can also work with multiple agents. 04 Can I edit what my agent creates? Yes. Everything remains editable on the canvas. You can drag, resize, style, animate and modify elements directly, then continue prompting from where you left off. 05 Does Recto generate real code? Yes. Recto uses HTML and CSS underneath your designs, making them easy to export and use outside Recto. 06 Does Recto require MCP or an API? No. Recto works locally with your coding agents without requiring MCP, API configuration or additional network calls between Recto and the agent. 07 Can I import existing designs? You can bring designs from websites into Recto. Figma import is coming soon. 08 How much does Recto cost? Recto is free. 09 Which platforms are supported? Recto is available for Mac, Windows and Linux. 11 Download Recto You both design. ## Questions
Fair questions.
Can you read my notes? No. Note text, titles, file and folder names, attachments and vault names are encrypted on your devices with keys the server never gets, on our servers and on yours alike. The server does learn some metadata, such as sizes, timing and who shares with whom; the security page lists exactly what.
Is anything kept for paying plans? No. Every plan, Free included, has every feature: the editor, drawings, sharing and editing together, comments, history, offline use, the command line and AI agents. Paying gets you more room, or a server of your own. Hosting it yourself, the only limits are the ones you set.
Can I try it first? Yes: the demo has people, shared vaults and notes in it already. Sign in as alice or bob, or any name, then open a second tab as someone else and edit together. Anyone can sign in as anyone there, and it starts over every hour, so keep nothing of yours in it.
What if I lose my phone and my laptop? Your recovery key, shown once when you set up, unlocks your account on a new device. Otherwise, new devices are approved from one you already use.
Can I take my notes and leave? Any time. Export a vault as Markdown, keep a synced folder of files on your disk, or export everything as one .zip and import it on another server: ours to yours, or back. Even without notekpr, an export and your recovery key are all you need to get your notes out as Markdown files.
Is it really open source? Yes, all of it, the server, the web app and the command-line client, under the AGPL. Read it, run it, check it: the docs explain how it's built and why.
Does it work with Obsidian? Yes. The command-line client keeps your vaults as a folder of Markdown that Obsidian opens as a vault, synced both ways. Importing an Obsidian vault brings its attachments and turns its Excalidraw drawings into drawings.
Does it work offline? Yes. The browser keeps an encrypted copy of your vaults, and what you write offline syncs and merges when you are back.
Is it ready? It's young, and it works: it is tested end to end, and known issues are tracked in the open. Hosted plans open soon; today you can try the demo or host it yourself. Keep backups of what matters, as with any new tool.

author: DRLogvinovich
body:
# README.md

- Branch: main
- Repository: Dr-Logvinovich/round-square

---

# Lean 4 Formal Proof: The Yang–Mills Mass Gap on Pure ℝ⁴ Is Ill-Posed, and on a Compact Constructible Manifold It Is Automatic (`RoundSquare.lean`)

Lean 4 Zero-Axiom CI
Zenodo Preprint DOI
Zenodo Concept DOI
ResearchGate DOI
Lean 4 Kernel
License: MIT

> **World's First Zero-Axiom Machine-Verified Negative-Result Resolution (Impossibility Theorem) of the Clay Millennium Yang–Mills Problem on Pure Non-Compact ℝ⁴.**
>
> * **Author:** Victor Logvinovich (Master of Physical and Mathematical Sciences; Researcher in Pedagogical Sciences (Mathematics), Kobrin, Belarus)
> * **ORCID:** 0009-0007-2040-6955
> * **Formal Verification Artifact:** `RoundSquare.lean` (3,705 lines, 31 Sections, 74 `#print axioms` checks, **0 `sorry`**, **0 `axiom`**, **0 `Classical.choice`**, **0 `propext`**)
> * **Full Manuscript Included:** `YM_V5.pdf` (*"The Yang-Mills Mass Gap on ℝ⁴ Is Ill-Posed, and on a Compact Constructible Manifold It Is Automatic"*, 38 pages, 14 figures)

---

## Executive Summary & Definitive Resolution Statement

For 26 years, the **Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problem** (*Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap*, Jaffe–Witten 2000) has asked for a single quantum gauge field theory on pure non-compact four-dimensional spacetime $\mathbb{R}^4$ that simultaneously satisfies two requirements:
1. **The Osterwalder–Schrader (OS0–OS4) and Wightman (W0–W4) Axiomatic Package (`OS` / "Round")**: Reflection Positivity, Källén–Lehmann Hilbert-space positivity, microcausal locality, a unique essentially self-adjoint local Hamiltonian $H$, and global holomorphic Cauchy–Wick rotation $\mathbb{R}^4 \leftrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{1,3}$.
2. **A Strict Spectral Mass Gap (`Gap` / "Square")**: $\Delta = \inf(\sigma(H) \setminus \{0\}) > 0$.

This repository contains the complete, self-contained **Lean 4 formal proof** (`RoundSquare.lean`) and the accompanying mathematical physics treatise (`YM_V5.pdf`) establishing the **final, terminal mathematical resolution** of this problem as posed on $\mathbb{R}^4$. In the exact foundational tradition of **Wantzel (1837)** on angle trisection, **Lobachevsky–Beltrami–Poincaré** on the parallel postulate, **Gödel (1931)** on incompleteness, **Turing (1936)** on undecidability, **Julia Robinson (1949) & Matiyasevich (1970)** on Hilbert's 10th Problem, and **Cubitt–Perez-Garcia–Wolf (*Nature*, 2015)** on the undecidability of the quantum spectral gap, we prove a machine-verified **Negative-Result Resolution** (Impossibility / Mutual-Exclusivity Theorem):

$$\mathrm{CanonicalPhysics}(\mathbb{R}^4) \;\land\; \mathrm{OS} \;\land\; (\Delta > 0) \;\Longrightarrow\; \perp$$

**This work does NOT attempt to construct a positive Yang–Mills measure on $\mathbb{R}^4$; instead, it formally proves WHY no such construction can ever exist, closing the $\mathbb{R}^4$ problem permanently.** Within the canonical constructive apparatus on pure non-compact $\mathbb{R}^4$, the axiomatic package (`OS`) and a strict mass gap ($\Delta > 0$) are **mutually exclusive conjuncts** ("a round square"):
* **Round forbids Square ($\mathrm{OS} \to \neg \mathrm{Gap}$):** Preserving the unbroken OS/Wightman axioms on infinite-volume $\mathbb{R}^4$ retains the uncut infrared continuum of long-wavelength modes $E(\lambda) = 1/(\lambda + 1)$, forcing a continuous spectrum $\sigma(H) = [0, \infty)$ and $\Delta = 0$ (`universal_continuum_no_rational_gap`, `universal_class_round_forbids_square`).
* **Square forbids Round ($\mathrm{Gap} \to \neg \mathrm{OS}$):** Enforcing a strict infrared mass gap $\Delta > 0$ on $\mathbb{R}^4$ requires cutting off the infrared tail via the Gribov horizon $\Omega$, the Fundamental Modular Region (FMR) $\Lambda$, and a global topological $\theta$-sector projector $P_\theta$ on the spatial boundary at infinity $S^3_\infty$, which simultaneously destroys OS2 Reflection Positivity, W0 Källén–Lehmann positivity, W4 Hamiltonian self-adjoint uniqueness, W3 Wightman microcausality (Strocchi's theorem), and Cauchy–Wick holomorphicity (`universal_five_concrete_hits`, `universal_class_square_forbids_round`).
* **Automatic Mass Gap on the Compact Constructible Manifold $M_{\text{tot}} = S^4 \times T^3$:** In Section 30 (`clay_conjunction_forces_not_nonCompact`), the Lean 4 kernel verifies that assuming $\mathrm{OS} \land (\Delta > 0)$ under Haag–Kastler–Strocchi gauge laws mathematically deduces $\neg \mathrm{boundaryS3Inf} \land \neg \mathrm{nonCompact}$. Abandoning the sterile $\mathbb{R}^4$ void for the compact constructible manifold $M_{\text{tot}} = S^4 \times T^3$ over the multiquadratic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5})$ removes $S^3_\infty$ at its root and yields an **automatic spectral mass gap** $\Delta \ge h(M_{\text{tot}})^2 / 4 > 0$ via Cheeger's inequality and the Lichnerowicz–Weitzenböck bound.

---

## Historical & Mathematical Lineage: From Julia Robinson (1949) & Hilbert's 10th Problem to Spectral Gap Undecidability (*Nature*, 2015) and `RoundSquare.lean`

 

> *"It is particularly ironic to watch superficial reviewers confuse the foundational 1949 arithmetic logic of Julia Robinson-whose paper laid the historical cornerstone for the negative resolution of Hilbert's 10th Problem-with 'machine-generated text.' Dismissing elementary Peano arithmetic and Diophantine order definability without reading the two-line inequality $\neg(q+2 \le q+1)$ is the ultimate proof that gatekeepers have stopped reading mathematics itself."*

To understand why the Yang–Mills Mass Gap problem on $\mathbb{R}^4$ is resolved by **Peano arithmetization** in `RoundSquare.lean` rather than by infinite-dimensional real-analysis hand-waving, one must trace the direct mathematical chain connecting **Hilbert's 10th Problem** to **quantum spectral gaps**:

### 1. Julia Robinson (1949) and the Negative Resolution of Hilbert's 10th Problem
In 1900, David Hilbert posed **Hilbert's 10th Problem**: find a universal algorithm that determines whether any given Diophantine equation has integer solutions. For 70 years, mathematicians searched for a positive construction.
In her landmark 1949 paper, *"Definability and decision problems in arithmetic"* (*Journal of Symbolic Logic*, 14(2), 98–114, 1949), **Julia Robinson** demonstrated that order relations and arithmetic predicates over rational and natural numbers ($\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{N}$) can be reduced to first-order existential/universal formulas in Peano and Diophantine arithmetic. Combined with the work of Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam, and Yuri Matiyasevich (the **MRDP Theorem**, 1970), this proved that Hilbert's 10th Problem has a **Negative-Result Resolution**: no such universal algorithm can exist, because Diophantine arithmetic encodes Turing's Halting Problem.

### 2. The 2015 Shock in Quantum Physics: Undecidability of the Spectral Gap (Cubitt, Perez-Garcia, Wolf, *Nature* 2015)
For decades, physicists assumed that Gödelian incompleteness and Hilbert's 10th Problem were purely abstract phenomena confined to mathematical logic, with no bearing on physical Hamiltonians.
In December 2015, **Toby S. Cubitt, David Perez-Garcia, and Michael M. Wolf** published their celebrated 140-page proof in *Nature* (*"Undecidability of the spectral gap"*, *Nature* **528**, 207–211, 2015):
* They proved that determining whether a quantum many-body Hamiltonian exhibits a **spectral mass gap** ($\Delta > 0$) or a **gapless continuous spectrum** ($\Delta = 0$) in the **thermodynamic (infinite-volume) limit** is **algorithmically undecidable**!
* How did they prove it? By encoding Turing's Halting Problem (and thus Hilbert's 10th Problem / Robinson–Matiyasevich Diophantine logic) directly into local quantum interactions: as the spatial volume goes to infinity ($V \to \infty$), no universal mathematical method can force a spectral gap to remain stable across the infinite-volume transition.

### 3. How `RoundSquare.lean` Completes this Chain for Continuum 4D Yang–Mills on $\mathbb{R}^4$
While Cubitt, Perez-Garcia, and Wolf (2015) established **undecidability** of the spectral gap across general infinite-volume lattice Hamiltonians, the Clay Millennium Problem fixes a specific continuum target: non-abelian $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills theory on infinite-volume non-compact $\mathbb{R}^4$ subject to the strict **Osterwalder–Schrader (OS0–OS4)** and **Wightman (W0–W4)** axioms.

In **Section 18** (`universal_continuum_no_rational_gap`) and **Section 29** (`unconditional_prize_level_physical_no_go`) of `RoundSquare.lean`, we apply Julia Robinson's exact 1949 method-**reducing rational order inequalities on $\mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ to bare Peano arithmetic on $\mathbb{N}$**:
1. **Peano Arithmetization of the Infinite-Volume Infrared Tail:** On non-compact $\mathbb{R}^4$, infinite spatial volume ($V = \infty$) supplies an untruncated sequence of long-wavelength infrared modes indexed by $\lambda \in \mathbb{N}$ with positive rational energies $E(\lambda) = \frac{1}{\lambda+1} \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$. Clearing denominators reduces the spectral lower-bound inequality $\Delta = \frac{p+1}{q+1} \le E(\lambda) = \frac{1}{\lambda+1}$ to the pure Peano relation `LeScale` on `Nat`:
 $$(p+1)(\lambda+1) \le q+1.$$
2. **The Elementary Peano Contradiction (`not_succ_leScale_self`):** Evaluating at the infrared mode $\lambda = q+1 \in \mathbb{N}$ yields $(p+1)(q+2) \le q+1 \implies q+2 \le q+1$, which collides unconditionally with the structural induction theorem $\forall m \in \mathbb{N},\; \neg(m+1 \le m)$. Because $\mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ (the Archimedean property), any putative real lower bound $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}} > 0$ sits above some rational $\frac{p+1}{q+1} > 0$ and is refuted by the exact same Peano step!
3. **From Infinite-Volume Undecidability to $\mathbb{R}^4$ Mutual Exclusion and Compact Decidability:** On pure non-compact $\mathbb{R}^4$, you cannot truncate the $\lambda \in \mathbb{N}$ tail without invoking the Gribov/FMR horizon ($\partial\Lambda \cap \partial\Omega$) or the boundary projector $P_\theta$ on $S^3_\infty$, which destroys the OS/Wightman axioms (`universal_five_concrete_hits`). Conversely, replacing non-compact $\mathbb{R}^4$ with the compact constructible manifold $M_{\text{tot}} = S^4 \times T^3$ over $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5})$ eliminates the infinite-volume limit ($V < \infty$, $S^3_\infty = \emptyset$), escaping the Cubitt–Wolf infinite-volume pathology and making the spectral gap $\Delta \ge h(M_{\text{tot}})^2 / 4 > 0$ **automatically decidable and strictly positive**!

## Official Clay Mathematics Institute (CMI) Specification & Resolution Status

In Section 6 (p. 6) of the official problem description, Jaffe and Witten state the requirement:
> *"Prove that for any compact simple gauge group $G$, a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills theory exists on $\mathbb{R}^4$ and has a mass gap $\Delta > 0$. ### Why This Formal Impossibility Proof Is the Complete & Final Mathematical Resolution
In mathematics, when a formal problem specification asks for an object $x$ in a domain $\mathcal{D}$ satisfying a conjunction $P(x) \land Q(x)$, there are only two possible deductive outcomes:
1. **Positive Construction (Sense i):** Exhibit $x \in \mathcal{D}$ such that $P(x) \land Q(x)$ holds.
2. **Negative-Result / Impossibility Resolution (Sense ii, Official CMI Rule on Counterexamples & Reformulations):** Prove that for all $x \in \mathcal{D}$, $P(x) \to \neg Q(x)$ and $Q(x) \to \neg P(x)$, demonstrating that the specification on $\mathcal{D}$ is over-determined ($\mathcal{D}(x) \land P(x) \land Q(x) \Rightarrow \perp$), and identify the exact domain reformulation $\mathcal{D}'$ where $P(x) \land Q(x)$ holds without contradiction.

Just as Gödel (1931) resolved Hilbert's second problem negatively by proving that no complete, consistent formalization of arithmetic can exist, Turing (1936) resolved the *Entscheidungsproblem* negatively, and Robinson–Davis–Putnam–Matiyasevich (1949–1970) resolved Hilbert's 10th Problem negatively, `RoundSquare.lean` and `YM_V5.pdf` resolve the Jaffe–Witten problem on $\mathbb{R}^4$ negatively and pair that impossibility proof with the positive spectral existence theorem on the compact constructible manifold $M_{\text{tot}} = S^4 \times T^3$ (Theorem 10.1, Corollary 10.4, and Section 12 of `YM_V5.pdf`).

title: Show HN: Search Everywhere at Once. Instantly
author: civnode
body: I've made AntiFind, to allow you to search everywhere at once, vastly increasing the efficiency of LLMs and your own searches:AntiFind indexes filesystems, not folders.It maintains a live view of storage by reading filesystem metadata directly. Because it understands the underlying filesystems, it can search across storage that the operating system is not currently exposing, including unmounted partitions.Allowing you to search for and play media from Linux in your Windows and the other way around. Without mounting the drives.This works on Linux, Windows and MacOS.The underlying idea is simple: instead of walking directories, read the filesystem's file tables directly.Most tools discover the filesystem again every time you search. AntiFind reads the drive's metadata in one pass and then follows changes as they happen.AntiFind supports Windows, Linux and macOS. It includes both a GUI and a command line. The CLI supports JSON output (--json) and was designed to integrate cleanly with automation and LLM workflows.There's a lot more to it, and you can find timings on my site, but that's the core idea.More information: https://antisoftworks.com/antifindCheers!

title: Show HN: FELF – AppImage-like single binaries without FUSE, root, or a runtime
author: Rucadi
body: Hello HN!I've always had a bad time redistributing programs that use shared libraries, AppImage in my opinion does too much, and a container is an overkill - not always integrates smoothly.I've moved to nix since long ago, but redistributing between nix and other distros or vice versa it's still a pain in the ass, more so if you want to run an alien app in nix or a nix app without the package manger in any other distro.For that, with the help of Claude, I've implemented a format that deduces at pack-time all the shared libraries a program needs, puts them, together with its own glibc and a patched dynamic linker into a single executable.This means that you don't actually need a runtime nor any special capability, it can run inside a FROM SCRATCH docker, alpine linux etc... And it also supports coreutils-like multiple programs accessible via symlinks, so it is a good fit for that purpose.You can just use:> felf pack $(which git) --output git.felfand you'll have already a git binary that works everywhere, no matter which distro you are building this from. This only packs the binary and their dependencies.Essentially, the effect is similar as if you LD_PRELOAD's all the libraries that it requires.In the end, we have been fighting these demons since long long ago, chroots/docker/appimage/flatpack/nix etc...So this xkcd applies: https://xkcd.com/927/I'm happy to share the project, I hope it inspires new discoveries/tools in this regard!

comments.author: Imustaskforhelp
comments.text: This is really beautiful from first glance.I had built appseed[0] inspired by zapps.app (curious what you think about that)and although, I could get some apps like bun and others to work statically using that. I struggled to make it work on things like OBS studio and it certainly had a lot of limitations with how it worked.It had a different approach of working where instead of pushing everything into a single binary, you had the .so file outside in an external filesystem of binary, could something like this work within FELF as well theoretically (for de-duplication purposes perhaps)?It seems that your experiment can work for almost every app including OBS and other complicated applications. I am rather really impressed by it and I will try to try it!I wonder if games can now be FELF'd as well and we can have containerized games into single binaries maybe, where I can just "run" games.What do you personally think could be the largest benefits of this approach and if there are any further things that you are pursuing in this area?This is really impressive work and thank you for releasing it! Have a nice day :-D[0]: https://github.com/serJaimeLannister/appseed

body:

 v1.0 GGUF

RESEARCH PREPRINT & OPEN-WEIGHTS RELEASE 
Run Gemma 4 26B 100% In-VRAM at 45.4 TPS on a 6GB Laptop GPU.
Manifold-Activated Pruning of Latent Experts (MAPLE) compresses 128-expert fine-grained MoE architectures down to 4.75 GB (1.48 effective BPW), eliminating PCIe system-RAM paging stalls forever.

Hardware Benchmark Proof
The PCIe Paging Death Spiral, Solved.
Consumer laptops cannot run uncompressed 26B models without overflowing into system RAM over bandwidth-constrained PCIe lanes.
Inference Throughput (RTX 4050 6GB) 
 6.57x Real-World Lift 
Base Gemma 4 26B IQ2_XXS (9.92 GB) 
 6.9 TPS (16/30 layers in VRAM) 
14 layers offloaded to system RAM. Constrained by 15.75 GB/s PCIe bus bandwidth.
MAPLE 48-Expert Container (4.75 GB)

100% In-VRAM execution. Dedicated 192 GB/s GDDR6 bus with zero host memory paging.

 Sub-2-BPW target architecture 
1.48 BPW

 Uncompressed 52GB -> MAPLE 4.75GB 
10.9x Compression 
Quality Parity: When the generation budget is set to 500+ tokens, MAPLE achieves 100% functional pass rate across syntax, logic, and data structure benchmarks with zero degradation compared to the unpruned base model.
Architectural Framing 
 Domain-Targeted Pareto Distillation 
We did not attempt lossy random pruning across the entire internet. Gemma 4 26B uses 128 fine-grained experts where massive clusters specialize in non-English languages, translation, and non-technical trivia. For edge code generation and technical deduction, those experts are dormant overhead.
MAPLE profiles the empirical activation manifold specifically on technical, algorithmic, and deductive tokens. We prune the 80 dormant experts and preserve the 48 active ones, masking excised router logits to -inf so softmax remains numerically stable.
Within the target domain (Python algorithmic synthesis, data structures, and logic), the model retains 100% functional unit-test execution when given standard token generation headroom (-n 512). The intentional trade-off is higher out-of-domain multilingual perplexity, which enables the model to run 100% inside 6GB VRAM at 45.4 TPS instead of stalling over PCIe at 6.9 TPS.
Architectural Foundation
Manifold-Activated Latent Profiling
Why naive expert removal destroys models, and how manifold activation analysis preserves technical reasoning.
Live Routing Profiling
MAPLE passes a multi-domain calibration corpus through Gemma 4, capturing exact token-to-expert router dispatch frequencies and activation magnitudes via llama-imatrix.
Dormant Expert Excision
80 dormant experts per layer are excised based on cumulative manifold energy thresholds. The router logits are dynamically re-indexed to dispatch across the 48 preserved experts.
GGUF Quantization Slicing
Preserved expert tensor slices are quantized into IQ2_XXS block representations using importance matrix weights, packaging the complete 26B model into a single 4.75 GB binary.
Empirical Reproducibility & Portability
Dynamic Calibration & Universal MoE Support
Pruning follows your activation manifold. Understand why your workload yields your model, and how to adapt MAPLE to any Sparse MoE architecture.
Empirical Calibration Reality 
Results Follow Your Calibration Corpus
MAPLE results are strictly deterministic and reproducible, but variable depending on your calibration dataset. What we released is a reference implementation on Gemma 4 26B-A4B optimized for edge technical execution.
Technical Specialization (Our Reference): Pruned 80 dormant experts, preserved 48 active ones. Reduced from 9.92 GB to 4.75 GB for 100% in-VRAM execution on 6GB GPUs.
General-Purpose Workloads: Calibrating on diverse multilingual dialogue activates a broad manifold. The optimizer may prune only 20 to 40 experts, retaining 88 to 108 experts for broad versatility.
Domain Customization: Biomedical, legal, or financial corpora activate entirely different expert clusters. If your workload is different, you get a different model.
"The reference Gemma 4 model proves the pipeline works. Your domain calibration produces your tailored edge container."
Universal SMoE Portability 
Theoretically & Practically Universal Across All MoEs
Because MAPLE operates on fundamental router logits and activation variance, the mathematical formulation is directly portable to any Sparse Mixture-of-Experts transformer:
Liquid AI LFM 24B MoE
Mixtral 8x7B / 8x22B
DeepSeek-V2 / V3 MoE
Qwen 2.5 MoE (57B-A14B)
Any model using top-k router gating can be profiled via llama-imatrix or PyTorch forward hooks, sliced, and masked to -inf without retraining.
Universal Recipe 
 How to Apply MAPLE to Any MoE Model (LFM-24B, Mixtral, DeepSeek) 
01. CALIBRATE 
 Assemble 2k-10k tokens of domain text representing your target operational workload.
02. PROFILE 
 Run llama-imatrix to capture activation frequencies and channel energy matrix.
03. SCORE 
 Compute composite score s = C * sqrt(sigma + eps) and rank active experts per layer.
04. MASK -INF 
 Excise unselected expert tensors and set excised router logits to -inf for softmax invariance.
05. DEPLOY 
 Quantize via llama-quantize (IQ2_XXS / Q4_K_M) for 100% in-VRAM execution.
Instant Local Deployment
Run in One Command
Native GGUF execution directly supported in llama.cpp, Ollama, and LM Studio.
bash - llama-cli 
Copy Command 
llama-cli -hf AmSach/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-MAPLE-Sub5GB-GGUF -ngl 99 -c 2048 -n 512 
-hf : Hugging Face repo auto-download
-ngl 99 : Offload 100% of layers to GPU
-c 2048 : 2k context window in 4.75GB

title: Show HN: Recalc – Spreadsheet where cells can be Claude Code or Codex terminals
author: sshah03
body: I built this because it was useful for me when building evals/benchmarks, and I decided to put it up for free for others. The goal was quite simple, make it easy to use a lead claude code / codex session in a panel on the side, while allowing every cell to also be a terminal session running claude/codex, and make it possible to continue a session in an actual terminal window if I needed to. They can all talk to each other using cells on the grid, named cells, or the MCP server that effectively glues the app together. I also found it useful for managing context within related but disparate sessions.My real benchmark runs with recalc are internal to my startup, so to demonstrate some of the functionality I built a small FDA Bench with the tool (obtain and put together dossier's of FDA submissions, and see if a harnessed Claude could have accurately predicted pass/fail): https://github.com/sshah03/recalc#a-model-benchmarkIt is still very much a work in progress, but given the versatility of spreadsheet apps, wanted to see how others see themselves using it and what doesn't exist that would be useful to them. Currently runs locally on macs, linux as well but that's less tested, and Windows hasn't been tested at all so that'll come in the future.

title: Show HN: Loop – your coding agents, from your phone
author: jamesasefa
body: Loop is a mobile-first companion workspace for the coding harnesses you already run. It aggregates results from your harnesses into a continuous feed that is easy to navigate and organize from your phone. I spent several months holding my newborn in one hand and trying to talk to agents one-handed on my phone. Every mobile UI is still based around chat, and it doesn’t scale on mobile, let alone one-handed!So I built Loop: a feed of the work your coding agents do. It’s built around agent results, not chats. You can scroll your history, get notified, save outputs, search and return to conversations later. The goal is to make interacting with agents via your phone feel familiar and intuitive based on the mobile UX we’ve all come to expect.Loop runs on your own computer — no account, no server, no app store — and pairs with your phone with one QR scan. It wraps the agents you already use (Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, Antigravity, Muse Code, Grok Build, or any ACP agent), each keeping its own context, tools, sign-in and billing — local models through Pi or OpenCode work too.Apache-2.0, TypeScript, SQLite. I'd love feedback from anyone else who builds from a phone.

author: kyisaiah47
body:
Aircheck Today Fix a post Wire your jobs Questions Docs 
 Connect Aircheck 
Aircheck shows every post your agents queued today on one screen. 
 Connect Aircheck See how a post is fixed 
 Claude Code Codex 
Aircheck reads the posts that your Claude Code, Codex, cron, Airflow and launchd jobs queued for the day and the ad creative that your ad pipeline builds. It shows each item with all of its media and whether it is ready to go out.
Review the whole day before posts go out.
 Aircheck offers a send-time strip, a thumbnail sheet grouped by hour, and a list. Each lane shows a ring until all of its posts are sent.
 The send-time strip places every post at its send time and colors it by platform. 
 The sheet shows the first image of each post, grouped by hour, with a slide count. 
 The list shows one row per post with its lane, format, send time, and file count. 
Aircheck provides three ways to work on a post.
 Each action runs the post's own pipeline again with a headless agent and shows the result beside the original.
 Example Shown only 
 Aircheck runs the post's pipeline again and shows a fresh version. It changes nothing.
Feedback Shown only 
 Write what should change. Aircheck shows the revised version beside the original and changes nothing.
Repair Can replace 
 Aircheck rebuilds the post through its pipeline. When you approve the new version, it replaces the queued post. Undo restores the old one.
Repair is off for sent posts and locks during the last minutes before a send. 
Aircheck works with the jobs you already run.
 Each job writes one JSON file per post into a queue folder. The MCP server writes those files, and your agent reports what it queued.
 The MCP server for Claude Code and Codex reads your setup, suggests the wiring, and applies it only after you approve it. You can also read the docs and write the files yourself.
 // queue/2026-11-06/blockdex-hero.json 
{
 "lane" : "brand-x" , 
 "at" : "2026-11-06T15:30:00Z" , 
 "kind" : "carousel" , 
 "text" : "Post copy as it will go out" , 
 "media" : [ "slide-1.png" , "slide-2.png" ] , 
 "status" : "queued" , 
 "postUrl" : null 
 } Read the full format in the docs 
Social posts and ad creative in one review.
 Social and Ads use the same screen. The screen shows the same day and media and provides Example, Feedback and Repair. Only the work changes.
 Social shows posts queued for your lanes, grouped by send hour. 
 Ads shows the creative built by your ad pipeline, grouped by the ad account it was cut for. 
 Repair replaces a queued post. Repair replaces an ad creative only while it is still a draft. 
Aircheck runs the agent on your machine, and a preview cannot post.
 Aircheck starts headless Codex or Claude as a local process. The agent can read your pipelines but writes only in its own run folder, and it has no network.
 Aircheck stores the JSON that describes your posts. It never stores your media. 
 Each run keeps the prompt it was given, its log, and its output. 
 Runs survive an Aircheck restart. 
Questions
 Does Aircheck post for me? No. Your jobs post. Aircheck shows what they queued and can replace a queued post only when you approve a repair.
Which agents does it run? Aircheck runs headless Codex or Claude on your own subscription and your own machine.
Can a preview go out by mistake? No. A preview runs with no network and can write only in its run folder. The prompt also forbids posting.
Can a repair make the problem worse? Press Undo. Aircheck backs up the old copy and files in the run folder.
Which platforms? Any platform your jobs post to. Aircheck reads the queue folder and does not connect to the platforms.
Review tomorrow's posts tonight.
 Install Aircheck and point it at your queue folder.

title: Show HN: Joggo – a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner for the Windows PC you use
author: AmirCat
body:
# telluric-dev/joggo

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-28T07:08:46Z

## Languages

- Dockerfile
- PowerShell
- Shell

## Topics

- claude-code-plugin
- github-actions
- homelab
- self-hosted-runner
- wsl2

## Top Contributors

- mindflyerio (6 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

A self-hosted GitHub Actions runner built to run for weeks on a machine someone is
also using.

Not a Kubernetes operator, not an autoscaler, not a fleet. One ordinary Windows PC
with 16 GB of RAM and WSL2, taking production builds since June 2026: one runner at
first, containerised runner slots since September, two of them from the end of September
and three since late October. Through clock drift, power loss, Windows Update reboots,
memory exhaustion down to 445 MB available, and a Docker daemon that occasionally stops
answering.

The code is maybe half of it. The other half is the comments: most files carry the
failure that produced them, what was measured, and what was tried and did not work.
That is deliberate. **`docs/memory-pressure.md` is the
single most useful page here** even if you never run any of this.

> **If you are an AI agent operating this box**, skip to
> For agents. It has the invariants, the paths, the
> safe/destructive command split, and the failure-mode discriminators in one place.

---

## Problems this solves

If you landed here from an error message, these are the ones joggo has a measured cause
and a working fix for. Each link goes to the write-up, whether or not you use joggo.

| You see | What it actually was |
|---|---|
| `i/o timeout` on `127.0.0.11:53`, `ENOTFOUND`, `Could not resolve host`, green on re-run | One lost DNS packet waiting out glibc's 5 s retry. docs/dns-packet-loss.md |
| `The token expired on …`, then `The runner registration has been deleted from the server` | WSL2's clock froze while the PC slept, so every OAuth token looked expired. docs/wsl2-clock-drift.md |
| Jobs queued forever, runner `active`, log silent, 0% CPU | A listener hung inside its token refresh. docs/recovery.md §3 |
| `The job was not acquired by Runner of type self-hosted even after multiple attempts` | GitHub's acquisition timeout racing the runner's restart between jobs. docs/memory-pressure.md §8 |
| `The self-hosted runner lost communication with the server` after a Windows Update | The reboot killed the job; joggo re-runs it. docs/operations.md |
| The PC runs out of memory and builds die, with no obvious culprit | Usually not the runner: a terminal emulator grew to 6 GB here. docs/memory-pressure.md |

---

## Why bother: the Actions bill

GitHub-hosted minutes are metered. Private repositories get a monthly allowance and
then bill per minute, and the rate is multiplied by the runner: Linux is the cheapest,
Windows costs several times more per minute, macOS more again. Check your own numbers at
**Settings → Billing → Plans and usage** — that page tells you what you are actually
spending, and whether any of this is worth your evening.

**Minutes on a runner you own are not metered at all.** You pay electricity and the
hardware you already bought. For a handful of repositories that rebuild a Docker image
on every push to `main`, that is usually where the bill is, and moving it to a desktop
that is idle most of the day removes it.

What this does **not** save, so the sums are honest:

- **Package storage and data transfer** are billed separately and are unaffected — you
 are still pushing images to GHCR.
- **Jobs that must stay hosted** keep costing what they cost. Anything needing
 `windows-latest` or `macos-latest` cannot move here; this is linux/amd64 only.
- **A monitor that watches your production service should not run on the box it shares
 resources with** — it will go red because the runner was busy, which is
 indistinguishable from the service being down. Leave that hosted.

And what it costs you instead:

- **The machine must stay on.** An asleep runner is a CI outage for every repository
 pointed at it.
- **It is slower per job, not faster.** Each job here pays 83–108 s of container rebuild
 at the handoff — measured, see Known limits. You are buying
 money back, not wall-clock.
- **You now own a security boundary.** A self-hosted runner executes whatever the
 allowed repositories tell it to, on your hardware, inside your network. Read
 `SECURITY.md` before the first install, not after.

---

## What you get

```
install.ps1 The installer: wizard for a human, flags for an agent, `-PreflightOnly` to
install/    check the box without touching it. WSL2 on Windows is the only target.
              CONTRACT.md                  config keys, flags, steps, exit codes

slots/      Two containerised runner slots. Each is a runner container plus its own
            Docker daemon, on its own network, with a throwaway work volume.
            run.sh --once per job, so no job ever sees another's workspace.
              run-containerized-slot.sh    the launcher (read its header first)
              add-slot.sh                  add slot N
              slot-pause.sh                drain/hold a slot without killing its job
              slots-status.sh              one-line state of every slot
              dind-image/                  the per-slot Docker-in-Docker image
              systemd/joggo-slot@.service  the template unit

guard/      Memory guard. Samples every 5 min and escalates: drop the VM page cache,
            then HOLD the slots so no NEW job starts while running jobs finish, then
            restart the VM only if the slots are idle.
              wsl-mem-guard.ps1            the guard
              mem-watch.ps1                the 5-minute sampler + snapshots

watchdog/   The three failure modes that actually took this runner down, each with a
            self-heal: a frozen clock that invalidates every OAuth token, a listener
            that hangs alive at 0% CPU, and a Windows Update reboot that kills an
            in-flight job.
              runner-watchdog.sh           wedge detector (65-min threshold; see docs)
              rerun-after-reboot.sh        re-dispatches jobs killed by a reboot
              take-restore-point.sh        ~450 MB rollback point before upgrades

monitor/    deploy-monitor.ps1   WPF monitor that reconstructs deploys from the
                                 runner's own journal. No GitHub token needed.
            day-report.ps1       daily "what failed, and why" page

network/    filter-aaaa.conf     dnsmasq drop-in for hosts that advertise AAAA
                                 records they cannot route (see Known limits)

tailscale/  acl.hujson           default-deny tailnet policy; admin devices, SSH only.
                                 OPTIONAL — only for managing a headless box remotely.

.github/    build-and-push.yml   reusable workflow_call image build (buildx → GHCR)
            node-test.yml        reusable containerised Node test job, with a
                                 no-host-port Postgres service
```

---

## Setup

**`docs/quickstart.md`** — shortest real path from nothing to a
green build. **Windows 10 2004+ or 11 with WSL2 is the only supported target**: every
Windows-side tool here (guard, sampler, monitor, day report) talks to the WSL VM from
the host, so there is no native-Linux or VM path.

```powershell
./install.ps1 -PreflightOnly                     # checks everything, changes nothing
./install.ps1 -Wizard                            # a human
./install.ps1 -NonInteractive -Json -Yes -Scope repo -Repo me/my-app -Token $env:JOGGO_TOKEN
```

`-Scope repo` is the **personal-account** path and is fully supported: runner groups are
an organisation-only feature, so a personal account registers the runner per repository
instead. `-Scope org -Org ` is the organisation path. Slots and the memory guard's
thresholds scale with RAM — 1 slot under 12 GB, 2 for 12–32 GB, 3 above; guard warn at
15% of RAM and critical at 7.5%, which is the measured 2500/1200 MB on a 16 GB box. The
honest floor is 8 GB. Tailscale is **optional** and only for remote management of a
headless box. Exit codes: `0` success, `1` failure, `2` bad usage, `3` preflight failed.

**The registration token is short-lived (~1 hour) and must never be committed or
stored.** Minting it is deliberately a human step — `SECURITY.md` and
`docs/recovery.md` §5 explain why automating it is left undone.

**The runner group — or, on a personal account, the set of repositories you registered
to — is the actual security boundary.** On an org, `Settings → Actions → Runner groups`:

```
Allow public repositories     MUST stay unchecked
Repository access             private repos only, chosen explicitly
Fork PR workflows             require approval for outside collaborators
```

**A self-hosted runner executes whatever the allowed repositories tell it to, on your
hardware, inside your network.** That list of repositories is the whole threat model.

To understand or deviate from any step, the long-form reference is
**`docs/runner-setup.md`**; to add a slot by hand,
`docs/adding-a-slot.md`. Neither pins a runner version: take
the current release, and the slot launcher resolves the installed runner's
version-stamped `bin`/`externals` symlinks at start rather than hardcoding a path.

### Then point a repository at it

Full runbook: **`docs/onboarding-a-repo.md`**. The fast
path calls the reusable workflow, which keeps a consuming repo to a few lines:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml in YOUR project repo
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['apps/**', 'packages/**', 'Dockerfile', 'package.json']
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  build:
    uses: <your-org>/joggo/.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml@main
    with:
      image-name: my-service        # defaults to the repo name
      context: .
      dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
      # publish-latest: false       # see the sharp edge below
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write               # REQUIRED for the job's GITHUB_TOKEN to push to GHCR
```

That is all. The reusable workflow already sets
`runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64, joggo]`, logs into GHCR with the job's own
`GITHUB_TOKEN`, and tags the image.

**One sharp edge, worth reading before you rely on `:latest`.**
`build-and-push.yml` appends `:latest` itself, gated on `enable={{is_default_branch}}`.
Two consequences:

- If your repo publishes **several** images and anything downstream keys off `:latest`,
 pass `publish-latest: false` and retag deliberately once every image for the commit
 exists. Otherwise the `:latest` pushes race each other.
- If your **deploy branch is not your default branch**, that gate never fires and
 `:latest` silently freezes. Check before trusting it:

  ```bash
  gh api repos/<owner>/<repo> --jq .default_branch    # vs the branch in your `on:`
  ```

 Equal → a separate retag job is redundant. Different → that retag job is the *only*
 thing publishing `:latest`, and deleting it breaks your deploys.

---

## Operating it

```bash
slots/slots-status.sh                       # what every slot is doing
slots/slot-pause.sh status --slot 1         # one slot, in detail
slots/slot-pause.sh pause  --slot 1 "why"   # drain: no NEW jobs; running job finishes
slots/slot-pause.sh resume --slot 1         # take jobs again
pwsh guard/wsl-mem-guard.ps1 -DryRun        # what the guard would do, changing nothing
```

Day to day: **`docs/operations.md`**.
When it stops taking jobs: **`docs/recovery.md`** — it opens with a
triage table, because the failure modes have *opposite* fixes and guessing makes things
worse.

---

## For agents — operating contract

If you are an AI agent asked to run or repair this box, this section is for you.

**Claude Code users: install the operator skills as a plugin.** They load the right runbook
for the problem at hand (supervising the box, a failed job, a runner not taking jobs, adding
a slot, risky upgrades):

```
/plugin marketplace add telluric-dev/joggo
/plugin install joggo@joggo
```

**There is a better version of this, specific to your box.** The installer renders
`agent/SUPERVISOR.md` to `C:\ProgramData\joggo\SUPERVISOR.md` with
the real distro name, paths, slot count and thresholds substituted — so it says
`-d Ubuntu-24.04` rather than `-d `, and `warn 2450 MB` rather than
`15% of RAM`. Paste that file as the opening prompt of a session that will supervise the
runner, or point the agent at it: it carries the standing duties, these invariants, the
command-safety split and the diagnosis tests, already resolved for one machine.

Rendered by default; `-NoAgentSupervisor` skips it. What follows is the generic form —
what you get reading the repo rather than running on a box.

### Invariants — do not violate these

| Invariant | Why |
|---|---|
| **No privileged secrets on the box.** No org-admin PAT; never store a registration token. | A self-hosted runner executes other repositories' code. See `SECURITY.md`. |
| **Never point a public repo, or fork PRs, at this runner.** | Arbitrary code on the operator's hardware, inside their network. |
| **A hold must never kill a running job.** `pause` writes a flag and the job finishes. Only `--now` interrupts, and it names the job first. | A hold that destroys work is worse than no hold at all. |
| **Ask before restarting the runner, the VM, or anything that drops a job.** | Hard to reverse, and the cost lands on other people's builds. |
| **Do not move the guard's thresholds to make a symptom go away.** | They came from measurements — see `docs/memory-pressure.md`. |

### Where state lives

```
/var/lib/joggo-slot/<N>.paused           the pause flag — the contract between
                                          slot-pause, the launcher and the guard
/var/log/joggo-slots/<N>/_diag/          that slot's Runner_*.log and Worker_*.log
C:\ProgramData\joggo\mem-watch.csv       the 5-minute sample trail
C:\ProgramData\joggo\snapshots\          full snapshots, written when free memory trips
C:\ProgramData\joggo\wsl-mem-guard.log   every guard decision, with its reasoning
```

### Command safety

```
READ-ONLY     slots-status.sh · slot-pause.sh status · wsl-mem-guard.ps1 -DryRun
              systemctl is-active|is-enabled · docker ps · journalctl
              gh run list · gh api .../jobs

MUTATING      slot-pause.sh pause|resume        reversible; loses no job
              systemctl restart joggo-slot@N    CHECK for an in-flight job first

DESTRUCTIVE   slot-pause.sh --now               kills the running job
              wsl --shutdown                    kills every job on the box
              config.sh remove                  deregisters; needs a fresh token
              ASK FIRST. Each of these costs somebody a build.
```

### Discriminators — read these before diagnosing

Several failure modes here are indistinguishable without the right test. These are the
tests, each learned by getting it wrong first.

**A job that never ran, versus a job that failed.** From the payload, no logs needed —
all four conditions together:

```
conclusion cancelled|failure · runner_name empty · steps 0 · labels include self-hosted
```

Every clause excludes a real case. *Zero **failed** steps* alone also matches a job a
human cancelled mid-flight, which reports its runner and its executed steps. Without
the `self-hosted` clause, every **hosted** job killed by a billing problem gets
misattributed to your runner.

**Queued forever — four causes with opposite fixes.**
`docs/recovery.md` has the table: clock drift (re-register), wedged
listener (restarting *is* the fix), Actions outage (do **not** restart), or the box
rebooted (already retried automatically).

**`--once` makes "inactive" normal.** A slot is genuinely `inactive` between every job.
Read `is-enabled` and the age of the newest `Runner_*.log` instead.

**A run's conclusion says nothing about whether anything was published**, in either
direction: a red run may have pushed its image already, and a green run may have
published nothing. Key off the publishing job, not the run.

**A read that cannot fail loudly returns a number, not an error.** Before trusting a
count, ask what the query would return if its basis were missing. If that is a
plausible number rather than an error, check the basis separately — with a positive
control in the same call, or the same quantity from a second instrument at a different
layer. `docs/memory-pressure.md` §9 has five instances from this box, every one of
which fooled somebody first.

---

## Three findings worth your time even if you close the tab

**`FreePhysicalMemory` is not free memory.** It is *available* memory — standby cache
plus free pages. The genuinely-empty portion swung between 3 MB and 4 GB on this box
within a day. Threshold on available; the other number is noise.

**This box runs 2× oversubscribed and has never paged out.** Committed memory sits at
26–33 GB against 16.3 GB of RAM, and `Pages Output/sec` was zero across ten days.
Memory compression absorbs it, paying in CPU rather than I/O — which makes
`pagefileMB` (a level, sticky for hours after a spike) the wrong signal, and the rate
the right one.

**The largest process on a CI box was a terminal emulator.** 24.2 MB/hour, dead steady
across 118 hourly samples, 6 GB by the end — bigger than the WSL VM. Nothing to do
with CI, and it eventually starved the runner into a seven-hour outage. If you build
monitoring, expect the answer to be something you were not watching.

---

## Status and honesty

Extracted from a working private setup, generalised, with organisation names and host
identifiers removed. It has run continuously for months in its original form.

**It has no CI of its own**, which is a slightly embarrassing thing for a CI project to
admit. The shell scripts pass `bash -n`; the reusable workflows are exercised daily by
real builds but are not validated in this repository.

**What has been run for real, end to end.** On a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 distro, Windows 11,
16 GB, as an ordinary user — **no elevation at any point** — against a real repository:

| | Result |
|---|---|
| Install, 2 slots | every step passes; verify reports 0 failures |
| Both runners online on GitHub | yes, and **still online 150 s after the installer exited** with nothing touching WSL |
| Re-run with `-Slots 1` | slot 2 retired: disabled, **deregistered**, root removed; slot 1 untouched |
| Install with everything on (guard, sampler, keepalive) | exit 0. Guard and sampler run as you and exit 0; the sampler's trail grows on schedule; the keepalive is still running 20 s and 150 s later; the guard reads the distro's live job count |
| Uninstall `-Deep` | 0 runners left on GitHub, 0 tasks, logs kept |

Not yet run: a reboot followed by logon (the tasks come back at logon by design), and any
machine other than the one this was extracted from.

Getting there found **more than twenty** defects. About ten stopped every install outright; the
rest left something broken behind. None was visible to a dry run. The ones worth knowing:

- **WSL's tunnelled DNS is unreachable from Docker's bridge**, so on a fresh install every
 container build failed at its first network step. The installer now writes Docker's DNS
 from the Windows adapters that are up, querying each before trusting it.
- **All WSL2 distros share one network stack.** Two runners in one WSL VM with the same slot
 subnet black-hole each other's traffic. The default subnet is now configurable, and the
 launcher refuses a subnet something else already routes.
- **WSL powers a distro off ~30 s after its last session closes.** Without a keepalive the
 runner passed verify and went offline when the installer exited.
- **A SYSTEM scheduled task cannot see your WSL distro** — distros are registered per Windows
 user. The installer used SYSTEM for the keepalive, guard and sampler, "so they work with
 nobody logged on"; the keepalive started and exited -1 within seconds. Every task now runs as
 you, at logon, like the guard on the original box. So the box must stay logged in (lock the
 screen), and the install needs no elevation.
- **The runner image runs as uid 1001;** a fresh `useradd` picks 1000, and every slot
 crash-looped on its first write. `ghrunner` is now created as 1001.
- **Text sent to the distro was re-encoded twice** (ANSI read, console-codepage pipe), so
 the Linux half of the installer could never be staged at all.

If you are the first to run it on another machine, especially the elevated path: please
open an issue with the transcript, pass or fail. That run is worth more than any review.

**Known limits, documented in place rather than in a tracker:**

- `--once` costs **83–108 s** of container rebuild per job, and GitHub's
 runner-acquisition timeout races it at *every* job boundary — so an 11-job workflow
 has eleven chances to die with *"not acquired by Runner of type self-hosted"*, not
 one. Measured on one repository: **~11% of jobs**. Persisting the Docker daemon and
 network while recreating only the runner container would recover most of it; that is
 not done here.
- **Nothing watches queue age.** A job that is never acquired looks exactly like a job
 that is merely slow.
- The Docker-in-Docker daemon is probed once at slot start and never again.
- Container memory limits are unset; the guard works at the VM level instead.
- The clock self-heal (chrony `makestep 1 -1`) ran on the original box but **the installer
 does not apply it**, nor install chrony. It is a manual step:
 docs/wsl2-clock-drift.md.
- `GET /actions/runs/{id}/jobs` returns only the **latest** attempt, so a green re-run
 erases the record of an earlier acquisition death. Any rate computed from it is a
 floor.
- Some hosts advertise AAAA records they cannot route, which makes build-time fetches
 and registry logins hang rather than fail fast. `network/filter-aaaa.conf` is the
 dnsmasq drop-in for that.

Issues and findings are both welcome — see `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
A measurement beats an opinion, and a method beats a measurement.

title: Show HN: Nino – Fastest C# serializer, safe on untrusted input, also TS/Go/Rust
author: jnx11
body: Nino is a source-generated binary serializer for C#, and as far as we know the fastest one. In the same BenchmarkDotNet run on GitHub runners against MemoryPack 1.21.4, it serializes classes and polymorphic types 3.5–7.2x faster and deserializes them 1.7–2.1x faster (arrays of unmanaged structs are on par). Deserializing into existing objects allocates nothing. Reproduce: https://nino.xgamedev.net/en/docs/v4/benchmarksIt is built to read bytes you do not trust: lengths are checked before allocating, depth is bounded, hash flooding is limited, and the read paths are fuzzed in CI.The bytes are a spec, not a memory dump, so CoreCLR, Mono, IL2CPP and 32-bit hosts write the same bytes, and runtimes for TypeScript, Go and Rust pass the same conformance corpus.Trade-offs: positional by default (VersionTolerant or Keyed for stored data), a 4-byte type id on polymorphic values, no System.Type, needs C# 9 and Roslyn 4.3+.Docs: https://nino.xgamedev.net

title: Show HN: Cross-device passkey auth on Android 9, synced with Bitwarden
author: riksnel
body: I saw a colleague log in to a website on my laptop by scanning a FIDO QR code. I wanted to do the same, but couldn't find a way to use the passkeys stored in Bitwarden on my phone to log in.So I asked Claude to build me an app. Claude found the task too daunting and only wanted to create a skeleton app. I was surprised by how complex the system actually is. Part of the process involves the phone sending an encrypted Bluetooth message as proof of presence, along with instructions on how to proceed.With the help of DeepSeek's free chat, I eventually managed to create a working implementation, after chasing quite a few hallucinations and dead ends... Claude then polished the app for me.The repository includes a full specification with test vectors, and the website has a nice, accessible explanation of how the process works.

comments.author: evanjrowley
comments.text: I'll try it. I've been looking for innovative passkey options for Android.One paint point with the Retroid Pocket 6, Nova, and (likely) the Duo, is they just don't support Passkeys. At least, this is how it seems. I've installed multiple Passkey-capable apps, tried with multiple web browsers, on multiple Passkey auth portals, and the passkey has never been detected. (This might be something I can solve with ADB and an LLM. Maybe that's all it is.)The point is, the passkey situation for many devices is suboptimal, and novel options like this could fill in an important gap. The gap is growing wider as Android handhelds with odd Android versions have grown in popularity.
