title: Show HN: After decades, I have my almost perfect music player
author: mococa
body:
# skhaz/overdrive

Music player for macOS. Synced lyrics, same volume for all songs, Last.fm scrobbles, and YouTube music videos.

- Stars: 4
- Forks: 1
- Watchers: 4
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-08T14:27:49Z

## Languages

- Shell
- Swift

## Topics

- lastfm
- lrc
- lyrics
- macos
- music-player
- swift
- swiftui
- youtube

## Top Contributors

- skhaz (345 contributions)
- AndreiRegiani (3 contributions)

---

## README

 

# Overdrive

GitHub release

A music player for the Mac (macOS 26 or later). It plays the music that is already on your Mac. You do not have to import anything.

Overdrive plays an album

## Features

- **Uses your music folders.** Add a folder and your albums show at once. New songs that you put in the folder show automatically.
- **Plays all common formats:** AAC, ALAC, MP3, FLAC, Opus, Vorbis, WAV, and AIFF.
- **Album covers** from your music files or from the image in the album folder.
- **Lyrics** that move with the song. If a song has no lyrics, the app finds them on the internet. You can also type and save your own, and show them in a small window that stays on top.
- **Similar artists.** With a Last.fm account, the lyrics panel gets two tabs: **Lyrics** and **Similar**. The Similar tab shows the ten artists most like the one that plays, with the cover of their most popular song, their name, their style, and their listeners. It loads them together and keeps its shape while they arrive, so nothing jumps. Click one to open its Last.fm page, or right-click it to copy its name. Staying on this tab through songs of the same artist keeps it; a new artist brings the lyrics back.
- **Same volume for all songs**, so you do not have to change the volume between songs.
- **Last.fm:** keeps a list of the songs that you listen to in your Last.fm profile.
- **Music videos from YouTube** in a small window that stays on top.
- **Discovery:** pick 1, 10, 20, or 100 songs at random from your library, only the songs you have not played yet, the ones you played most, or the top tracks of your Last.fm artists and of your own top bands.
- **Play counts:** every song shows how many times you played it all the way through, and you can sort any list by it. The counts travel with your music. **Addicted** in the sidebar (a flame) collects your twenty most played songs in one list, best first, current the moment you open it.
- **Playlists** and **Up Next** (the list of what plays next). Up Next in the sidebar shows the song that plays and the songs that come after it. Add songs to it from the menu of a song; they play right after the song that plays, and many picks at once keep their order. Drag them to change the order, or press Delete to remove them. Clicking a song further down the list does not throw the songs above it away: they stay where they are, still marked as not played, and the player reaches them after the song you clicked finishes. A song only leaves the list when it played, or when the player passed it. When the last song of the list ends, or you press Next on it, the list is done and its songs leave Up Next, so Play does not start them again. Click the trash button to clear the list. After you confirm, the song stops and the player starts again with no song.
- **Liked songs.** Like any song and find them all in **Liked Songs** in the sidebar. With a Last.fm account, your likes and your loved tracks stay the same list, in both directions.
- **Continues where you stopped.** When you open the app again, it shows the same song, at the same time.
- **Keyboard media keys** and Control Center play, pause, and change songs.
- **Apple Music does not open by accident** while you use Overdrive.
- **Song details:** the quality and the size of each song file.
- **Mp3tag:** if you have Mp3tag, you can open your songs in it to edit their names and details.

## Install

Install Homebrew, open Terminal, and type:

```sh
brew install --cask skhaz/tap/overdrive
```

## How to use

### Add your music

Drag a music folder to the window, or choose Overdrive > Settings > Folders > Add Folder. You can add more than one folder. The app also finds the songs in the folders inside it.

### Find and play

- Use the sidebar to see **Albums**, **Artists**, or **Songs**.
- Type in the search field to find an artist, an album, or a song. The search stays until you clear it with Escape, Command-K, or the clear button.
- To go back to the previous screen, click the back arrow at the top, press Command-[, or swipe to the right on the trackpad. To go forward again, click the forward arrow, press Command-], or swipe to the left. The side buttons of a mouse also work.
- Double-click a song to play it. On an album, click **Play** or **Shuffle**.
- Click a column title (Title, Artist, Album, Time) to sort a list. Click again to reverse the order, and a third time to go back to the order of the list. When you leave a list or quit the app, the list goes back to its own order.
- Albums go from the oldest to the newest.
- Use the bar at the bottom to play, pause, go to the previous or next song, shuffle, repeat, go to a different part of the song, and change the volume.
- Click the cover or the name in the bottom bar to open the album that plays.

The song that plays shows in color and is selected in the list.

### Discover songs

The **Discovery** menu at the top of the screen has five pickers, each with 1, 10, 20, or 100 songs:

- **Songs** picks that many songs at random from your whole library.
- **Never Played** picks only the songs you have not played yet.
- **Most Played** picks from the songs you played, and takes the ones with the highest count.
- **Last.fm Artists** asks Last.fm for the artists you listened to most, takes a group of them at random, and for each one draws a song from its five most played that your library really has.
- **Top Bands** does the same, but it picks the bands by your own play counts instead of what Last.fm thinks you like.

The two Last.fm pickers open the Up Next page the moment you click them and show a spinner in the middle of the list when they take more than a fifth of a second, so you can see that they are working. When a picker adds nothing, the list says why in a line at the bottom, and you clear it with its x. The app puts the chosen songs in Up Next and plays the first one right away, then opens the Up Next page so you see the list. What was in Up Next before goes away. A new discovery replaces the one before it, also while one is still on its way: an answer that arrives late is dropped, and the list you chose last is the one that plays. Each local picker shows how many songs it can pick from, and a value that needs more songs than that is dimmed, so you never get a shorter list than you asked for. The pick never follows the search: it reads the whole library.

**Infinity** is the endless mode at the end of the same menu. Turn it on and the app starts a list of 20 songs and keeps 20 more queued for as long as you play: every song is one you have, drawn from the five most played tracks of an artist of your library that Last.fm ranks highest, and a new batch is asked for quietly when the song that plays reaches its half. You never see it work: the songs go to the end of Up Next, the one that plays is never touched, and the list is never reordered. An artist whose songs all played leaves the draw, so nothing repeats before your library is empty, and then the cycle starts again. Turn it off, or start any other list, and the mode stops; the songs it already queued stay in Up Next.

**Banned Songs** is in the sidebar, under **Liked Songs**. It lists every song you banned, and it is the way back in: select the rows and press Delete, or right-click them and choose **Unban Song in Discovery**. Only the ban goes away, never the song, its tags, or its place in your library. The list lives in `Bans.plist` next to your likes and playlists, so it travels with the folder.

The two Last.fm pickers and **Infinity** need the Last.fm key built into the app and your account connected in Settings > Last.fm. Without either one they are dimmed, and **Top Bands** is also dimmed while no song has a count. Every click asks the internet again; the app keeps nothing from Last.fm on the disk. The artists are drawn at random from five times the number of songs you asked for, so the same names do not always win. For each artist the app asks Last.fm for the artist's most played songs and keeps the ones your library really has. Last.fm ranks its own list by how many people listened, not by how many times a song was played, so the app asks for a wide page of 20 and keeps the five with the most plays: if you have only one of them, that song goes into the list; if you have more than one, the app draws one of them at random. An artist whose top five you do not have at all is skipped, so every song of the list is one you have. It asks for four artists at a time, so a discovery of 100 songs is many requests, and Last.fm answers too many requests from one address for a short while with an error. When that happens the list is simply shorter, or empty, and the app changes nothing and says so in the log. While one of them is on its way, both are dimmed, so you do not spend two searches at once.

A song matches a Last.fm title by name: the app compares the letters and digits of the two names, so accents, case, punctuation, and spacing make no difference, and it takes the title when the names are at least 80% alike. A long suffix is a different song: "Come As You Are" does not match "Come As You Are (Remastered)", and "Sandman" does not match "Enter Sandman", while "Sandman" does match "Sandmen". The app plays the name your library has, not the name Last.fm sent.

### How many times a song played

Every song shows how many times you played it. A play counts when you hear about 80% of the song, so a song you skip halfway does not count, and a song that reaches its end always counts. The number is in the **Plays** column of **Songs**, **Up Next**, your playlists, and **Liked Songs**, and next to the time of each song in an open album. Click **Plays** to sort by it: once for the least played first, again for the most played first, a third time for the order of the list. **Never Played** in Discovery is the same count: a song with a number above zero never shows there.

The counts live in a **Plays.plist** file at the root of your first music folder, so they move with your music. A count is for a song, not for a place on the disk: the file knows a song by its name, album, and artist. If you change the album or the artist of a song, its count starts again at zero. The app writes the counts once an hour and when you quit, so a crash can lose the plays of the last hour.

### Use the menu of a song

Right-click a song, an album, or the bottom bar. You can:

- **Add to Up Next** (the songs play next, right after the song that plays).
- **Add to Playlist**.
- **Watch Video on YouTube**.
- **Go to Album** or **Go to Artist**.
- **Copy** the song name, the artist, the album, or "Artist - Song Name".
- See the **Information** of the song file. Click an item to copy it.
- **Open in Mp3tag** or **Show in Finder**.

- **Ban Song in Discovery** (or **Unban Song in Discovery** for a song you already banned). The song stays in your library, stays in every list, and plays whenever you choose it, but no discovery and no Infinity picks it again. The app asks you to confirm. The item is in the menu of every list of songs: Songs, an album, Up Next, a playlist, Liked Songs, and Banned Songs.

To do this for more than one song, select the songs with Command-click or Shift-click, then right-click one of them.

### Make playlists

1. Click **+** in the sidebar, or choose File > New Playlist.
2. Right-click songs or albums and choose **Add to Playlist**.
3. Drag the songs in the playlist to change the order.
4. To remove a song, right-click it and choose **Remove from Playlist**, or press Delete.

To delete a playlist, right-click it in the sidebar. The playlists live in a Playlists folder inside your music folder, with a backup copy, so they move with your music.

### Like songs

Click the heart in the bottom bar to like the song that plays. You can also right-click any song or album and choose **Like Song**. A heart shows next to each liked song in the lists.

Click **Liked Songs** in the sidebar, below Songs, to see all liked songs. To remove a like, right-click the song and choose **Unlike Song**, or click the heart again while the song plays.

#### Keep your likes in step with Last.fm

If you connected your Last.fm account in Settings > Last.fm, your liked songs and your Last.fm loved tracks are the same list. A like you make in Overdrive goes to Last.fm. A love you make on the Last.fm site, or in another player, comes to Overdrive.

A like you make in the app is on your disk at once and on its way to Last.fm in the same second, so it is there with or without the internet. With no Last.fm account connected, a like is only a liked song in Overdrive: no request, nothing kept for later that could grow. The moment you connect the account, the app sends the likes you made and brings your loved tracks down. With no network, the like waits in a queue on the disk and goes up the moment the network comes back; the app also retries it by itself every minute, so it never waits for the next sync. A like leaves the queue only after Last.fm answers that it took it, so an error page or a server that is down never counts as a success.

The app syncs when it opens, every minute, when the network comes back, and when you connect your account. A minute is the longest the two lists can disagree: a love or an unlove made in the app, or on the Last.fm website, is in the other list in about a minute without a click. A sync is one request: Last.fm lists your loved tracks newest first, so the app reads the top of the list and stops at the song it already knows, and it checks the count Last.fm reports. Only when that count says something changed below — a song you loved or unloved on the site — does it read the whole list, which costs two requests instead of one. To read the whole list at once, choose **File > Sync Liked Songs from Last.fm**, or **Sync Loved Tracks Now** in Settings > Last.fm: both read the list page by page until the end. Settings also shows how many loved tracks Last.fm holds and how many of your wishes are still waiting to go up.

A song is matched by its artist and title, not by where the file is, so moving your music folder does not break the list. The two lists are one list in both directions: a song that Last.fm loves and your library cannot play is unloved on Last.fm, so nothing stays loved there without a song here. The app only does that after a complete scan of a library with a readable folder, so a drive that is not mounted, or a scan that failed, never takes your loves away. A song your library holds under another spelling is loved, never unloved, and the app says the name Last.fm keeps when it changes that song. Last.fm can be a few seconds behind your own change, so the app protects a like or unlike you just made for one read: a stale answer cannot undo it. If a sync cannot read your whole loved list — no network, a partial answer, or more than 20 000 loved tracks — it changes nothing at all and tries again later, rather than treating a short answer as a list of unlikes.

The wishes that have not gone up yet live in `Loves.plist` inside `~/Library/Application Support/Overdrive`, so a crash or a quit loses nothing. Unlike the play counts, this file is about your account and not about a folder, so it does not travel with your music.

### Lyrics

The lyrics show at the right side when a song plays, and they always show the song that plays: picking another song in a list does not change them. Click a line to go to that part of the song. To change the lyrics, click **Edit** (Command-E) and type. The app saves the lyrics next to the song by itself, and **Save Lyrics** (Command-S) writes them at once. If the app cannot write the file, it asks **Save** or **Discard** when you click **Done**, so an edit is never lost without a question. To remove the lyrics, delete all the text. The lyrics that the app finds on the internet stay next to the song, in a file with the `.cache.lyrics` extension, for one month. After that the app looks for them again and keeps the old ones if it finds nothing new. To keep the lyrics that the app finds on the internet, edit them.

To hide the lyrics, click the lyrics button in the toolbar (Option-Command-Y). Click it again to show them. While the lyrics are hidden, the app does not look for them. The app remembers your choice.

Click the undock button at the top of the lyrics to move them to a small window that floats above all other windows. The window shows the album cover, the song, the artist, and the album. It also has the play controls: previous, play or pause, next, and a slider for the position of the song. You can edit the lyrics in the window too. Drag the window to move it. It keeps the lyrics when the next song plays. Click the X in the window to put the lyrics back in the app.

To float the lyrics of the song that plays at any time, choose Controls > Show Lyrics in a Floating Window (Command-U). It works for every song, even when the song has no lyrics.

### Watch the music video

1. Right-click a song and choose **Watch Video on YouTube**.
2. The first time, sign in to your Google account in the window. Passkeys do not work in this window, so click **Try another way** and use your phone, or your password and a code.
3. The video plays in a small window in a corner of the screen. The song in Overdrive pauses.

Drag the window to move it to a different corner. Put the pointer on the video to see the close button. When you play a song in Overdrive, the video window closes.

### Connect Last.fm

Choose Overdrive > Settings > Last.fm. Type your Last.fm username (not the email) and password, and click **Connect**.

When you are connected, the menu bar shows a **Last.fm** menu: **Go to Profile** opens your account in the browser, and **Go to Artist** and **Go to Album** open the pages of the song that plays. The app asks Last.fm for the spelling it keeps, so the page is the right one even when your tags spell the name differently; when Last.fm does not know the name, it opens the Last.fm page of that name, which says it was not found. Without a connected account the menu is not there.

### Settings

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Folders | The folders with your music. |
| Playback > Show Spectrum | Show or hide the bars of the song that plays, above the playback controls (default: shown). |
| Last.fm | Connect or disconnect your Last.fm account, see your loved tracks, and sync them now. |
| YouTube > Open Videos In | Show the videos in the small window (default) or in your web browser. |
| YouTube > Window Corner | The corner of the screen for the video window. |
| YouTube > Sign Out | Sign out of YouTube. |

To turn off the same volume for all songs, choose Controls > Normalize Volume.

### Keyboard shortcuts

The Song menu at the top of the screen has the same actions as the right-click menu, for the selected songs or album. The menus show the shortcut of each action that has one.

| Keys | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Up Arrow, Down Arrow | Go to the previous or next item |
| Shift-Up Arrow, Shift-Down Arrow | Add the previous or next song to the selection |
| Left Arrow, Right Arrow | Go to the previous or next album (when the search field is empty) |
| Return | Open the album or the artist, or play the song. If the song plays, pause it |
| Space | Play or pause (when the search field is empty) |
| Escape | Close the video. Stop to edit the lyrics. Clear the search. Go back |
| Delete | Remove the selected songs from the playlist, or delete the selected playlist in the side bar |
| Tab | Go between the side bar and the main area |
| Command-[ | Go back to the previous screen |
| Command-] | Go forward again |
| Control-Return | Open the menu of the item, as with a right-click |
| Command-Return | Add the selected songs to Up Next, to play next |
| Shift-Command-L | Like or unlike the selected songs |
| Shift-Command-Y | Watch the video of the selected song on YouTube |
| Shift-Command-N | New playlist with the selected songs |
| Shift-Command-R | Show the selected songs in Finder |
| Command-Delete | Remove the selected songs from the playlist |
| Command-Right Arrow | Next song |
| Command-Left Arrow | Previous song |
| Option-Command-Right Arrow | Go forward 10 seconds |
| Option-Command-Left Arrow | Go back 10 seconds |
| Command-Up Arrow | Increase the volume |
| Command-Down Arrow | Decrease the volume |
| Command-L | Show the album of the song that plays |
| Option-Command-L | Like or unlike the song that plays |
| Option-Command-S | Shuffle on or off |
| Option-Command-R | Repeat: off, all songs, or one song |
| Command-E | Edit the lyrics |
| Command-S | Save the lyrics |
| Option-Space | From any app: open Overdrive and search |
| Command-U | Show the lyrics in a floating window |
| Option-Command-Y | Show or hide the lyrics |
| Command-N | New playlist |
| Command-R | Look for new music in your folders |
| Command-K | Clear the search |
| Command-, | Settings |
| Media keys | Previous song, play or pause, next song |

## Good to know

- Click **About** at the top of the sidebar to see the version of the app and to open its page on GitHub, report a problem, or see the releases. The page also checks GitHub for a new version and shows a link when there is one. If GitHub does not answer, the page shows nothing more.

- The app never changes your songs. It only saves the lyrics that you save.
- Your liked songs, playlists, and lyrics live with your music. Back up your music folder and you back up all of them.
- The app keeps a file named `Cache.sqlite` in each music folder. With it, the app opens faster. You can delete it at any time: the app makes it again. The app checks your music folders by itself when they change and every 10 minutes. To check them at once, choose File > Sync Library (Command-R). If you change the tags of a song with an app that keeps the file date, choose File > Rebuild Library Cache: the app reads all your songs again. Until it finishes, you see the library as it was.
- When you play an album in order, the quiet and loud songs of the album stay as the artist made them.
- No Last.fm play is lost. With no internet, every play waits in a queue on the disk and goes up when the network comes back, at once and again every minute. A play leaves the queue only after Last.fm answers that it took it, so an error page or a server that is down never counts. With no account connected, a play is not a scrobble and the app does not keep one; your play counts still go up.
- The video window opens at once, and you stay signed in to YouTube.
- YouTube can show an ad. With YouTube Premium, there are no ads.
- If something goes wrong, the app keeps a log of the last day in `~/Library/Logs/Overdrive`. Send it with your bug report.

## Credits

- App icon: “iPod Orange” by p_bluealt, from macOSicons. The MIT license does not apply to the icon.
- Lyrics: LRCLIB and lyrics.ovh.
- Scrobbles: Last.fm.
- Music videos: YouTube.
- GitHub mark on the About page: Primer Octicons (MIT). GitHub and the GitHub logo are trademarks of GitHub, Inc.

The About page in the app shows the same credits, with the same links.

title: Show HN: OfflineVault – AI based offline library for when the internet is down
author: nc
body:
OfflineVault 
Library 
 Answers 
 Accuracy 
 Pricing 
 Questions 
 Download 
Library 
 Answers 
 Accuracy 
 Pricing 
 Questions 
 Download for Mac 
For the week the internet is gone
When the internet is gone, the answers are still here.
A week without power. No bars after the storm. Someone hurt and no one to call. The water, food, first aid, medicine and repair answers you used to search for are already on your Mac, each one with the page it came from, and they work with Wi-Fi off.
Download for Mac, free 
 See what's inside 
Tested on 150 emergency questions. With the default model: 63 fully right, 73 partly right, 4 wrong, 0 harmful. Every wrong answer is published. 
Apple Silicon, macOS 14 or later
Free tier, no account
Open source, GPL-3.0
Linux and Windows through ovsync 
When you'd use it
Built for moments like these.
Each of these is a question you would have typed into a search box. Here is what happens instead.
Day three with no power.
 Is the food in the fridge still safe? The Field Guide article opens first, word for word, with the FEMA page it came from. The assistant's own words come after, in a lighter style.
Someone is bleeding and 911 is not answering.
 Ask how to make a tourniquet from a belt. Every step carries a number. Click it and the Army first aid manual opens at that page, with the passage marked.
The phone has no bars.
 A child is shivering after a night without heat. Search "hypothermia child" and one list shows the medical article, the manual page and the video you saved. No internet, and no assistant needed.
The tap runs dry.
 Open the No safe water card. Six steps, each one checked against the CDC page it came from. Tick them off on screen, or print the card before the power goes.
What's on your Mac
The shelf, by situation.
Start with the Field Guide. It is free, a person wrote it, and every step names the manual it came from. The reference books behind it are the deep shelf.
Free, no account 
 The OfflineVault Field Guide: 95 articles on water, fire, first aid, medicines, food, shelter, power, hazards, evacuation, children and the elderly, hygiene, communications, navigation, mental health and pets. Beside it, CDC emergency preparedness, Ready.gov from FEMA, the US government preparedness manuals, MedlinePlus, the iFixit repair manuals and a map of the whole world. 
 Hurt or sick 
 WikiMed, the medical side of Wikipedia. WikEM, the emergency room wiki. MDWiki. The US military medicine manuals. The NHS Medicines A to Z, so you can look up what a pill does and what it must not be mixed with. Core plan. 
 Fix, grow, build 
 Appropedia for low-tech water, cooking and power. The Sustainable Living, Outdoors and Electrical Engineering Stack Exchanges. Wikipedia's top 50,000 articles. Core plan. 
 Everything 
 All of Wikipedia with pictures, about 127 GB. The whole world at street level, about 139 GB. Wikibooks, Wikivoyage, Wiktionary, Project Gutenberg's medicine, farming and military shelves, and thirteen more Stack Exchanges, on gardening, home repair, car repair, cooking, parenting and ham radio among others. Household plan. 
 Yours 
 Drop in PDFs and EPUBs, save web pages, keep YouTube channels with their subtitles. All of it lands in the same search. 
Every file is checked after download, and every book shows the month its copy was made. The full list, with the licence of every title, is on the Sources page .
How it answers
It shows you the page. It won't guess.
The assistant is a reader, not an expert. It answers only from the books on your Mac, and under every claim it shows the exact passage it read.
It shows the page 
 Every numbered claim opens the document at the page, with the passage it quotes. Medical, electrical and structural answers end with a reminder to read the source yourself. 
 It marks what it can't prove 
 A sentence with no passage behind it is labelled unverified, so you can tell the quote from the guess. 
 It says no 
 A child's medicine dose. Whether a mushroom is safe to eat. How much bleach to mix. It will not answer these from memory. It refuses, says why, and points you to the packaging, a pharmacist or the manual. 
 For the dangerous questions, no model at all 
 Bleeding, burns, poisoning, a chemical release. When a Field Guide article covers the question, the app shows that article alone and never asks the assistant. 
We ask it 150 questions a person might type in an emergency, through the real app, and score the answers with a fixed rule, not another model. The default model got 63 fully right, 73 right but missing a listed fact, 4 wrong and 0 harmful, and it refused 10 of the 10 questions it should refuse. Muse Glimmer 30B, the biggest model Household offers, got 74 fully right and 0 harmful. Every wrong answer is printed in full. 
Also on your Mac
Maps, videos, and a drill that proves it.
Everything here runs with Wi-Fi off. Run the drill before you need it.
The whole world, offline
 Pan anywhere. Click for coordinates you can read over a radio, or type them to jump. Download street detail for the area on screen, or the whole planet at street level (139 GB).
Videos with transcripts
 Keep the channels you trust. The transcript sits beside the player, searchable, and the assistant can quote it.
A drill that proves it
 One button checks every book, every file, the maps, the assistant, your backup and your free space, with Wi-Fi off. Anything amber gets a fix button.
Phones in the house get it too
 Switch on Share on Wi-Fi and every phone on your network can read the library from the Mac. Read-only, off by default, included with Household.
Linux or Windows
No Mac? Take the library anyway.
ovsync is a small command-line tool, open source like the app. Give it your key and it downloads the same checked library into a folder Kiwix can serve. Without a key it downloads the free shelf.
pipx install "git+https://github.com/nc/offlinevault.git#subdirectory=ovsync"
ovsync activate OV-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX
ovsync sync ~/offlinevault
kiwix-serve --port 8080 --library ~/offlinevault/library.xml 
 It checks every file after download, resumes an interrupted download, and writes a library.xml for kiwix-serve, kiwix-desktop or a phone pointed at a shared drive. The code is on GitHub , with the source page .
What people ask before they buy.
Can't I just use Kiwix? Yes, and most of the shelf is Kiwix content. The app is free and open for exactly that. What you pay for is a shelf someone else gathers, checks and refreshes every month, plus the Field Guide, the maps, the videos and a search that quotes the page.
What if it's wrong? It can be. So we test it on emergency questions through the real app, score the answers with a fixed rule, and publish every wrong one. Today that is 4 of 150 wrong and 0 harmful with the default model. The page it quotes is always one click away. See the results. 
What if I stop paying? Nothing you downloaded is taken away. The books, the maps and the assistant keep working from your drive with no time limit, and you can export all of it. You only stop getting new editions.
Why a Mac app? The assistant runs on the Mac's own chip, so an answer needs no server and no internet. One app holds the books, the maps, the videos and the search. No Mac? ovsync puts the same library on Linux or Windows for Kiwix.
Is my data private? Nothing you read, ask or search leaves your Mac. There is no telemetry, and the free tier needs no account. The app talks to our servers only to download content, check for an update and confirm a licence key. The whole policy. 
How big is it? The free shelf is about 8 GB. Core adds about 19 GB and fits on the Mac's own drive. The complete library is about 476 GB and wants an external SSD. You pick what to download.
Pricing
Buy it once. Keep it forever.
Free is a real option. Core is the one most households need. Either way, everything you download stays on your drive and keeps working, plan or no plan.
Free $0 
The app, the Field Guide, CDC and FEMA preparedness, the US government manuals, MedlinePlus, the iFixit manuals and the world map. No account, no key.
Download for Mac 
Core
 $149 once 
 a year of new editions included, then $39 a year only if you want them
Everything in Free
 WikiMed, WikEM, MDWiki
 Military medicine, NHS Medicines A to Z
 Wikipedia's top 50,000 articles
 Appropedia and three Stack Exchanges
 The assistant, 4B model
 New editions every month
 2 Macs, email support
Buy Core 
Household
 $249 once 
 a year of new editions included, then $59 a year. Everything in Core, plus
All of Wikipedia with pictures
 The whole world at street level
 Bigger assistant models
 Wi-Fi sharing for the household
 Up to 6 Macs
Buy Household 
Founder, $299 once, at launch only. Three years of Household, Core for life, your name in the credits. Join as a founder . Already have a key? Refresh it for another year .
If you stop paying
New editions stop. That is all. The books, the manuals, the maps and the assistant keep working from your drive, you can export every file, and the free shelf still updates. Want new editions again? Refresh the same key for a year, whenever you like.
Download
Put it on your Mac today.
The app is free. Install it, run the drill with Wi-Fi off, and decide about a plan after.
Download for Mac 
macOS 14 or later, Apple Silicon
Notarized by Apple
Free tier, no account
Not ready yet?
Leave your email and the plan you are weighing. One message when there is real news, nothing else.
Core Household Founder Free 
 Keep me posted 
Questions
The practical ones.
Does it really work with no internet? Yes. After the first download every part runs on your Mac. The Readiness drill is there so you can prove it yourself with Wi-Fi off, before the day you need it.
What is a refresh? A new edition of each book, pack and map as its source changes, published monthly. Core and Household include a year of them. After that, $39 a year for Core or $59 for Household keeps them coming, billed yearly on the same key until you cancel. Nothing you downloaded depends on it.
What happens if I let the refreshes lapse? New editions stop. Everything you downloaded keeps working, with no time limit, you can export all of it, and the free shelf still updates. Refresh the same key whenever you want new editions again.
Can I trust it with medical questions? Treat it as a librarian, not a doctor. It answers only from books you can open, shows the page, flags medical topics, and refuses where a guess could hurt someone. Then read the page.
Why does it sometimes answer only with the Field Guide? Because for some questions a quote is safer than a summary. When a question is about bleeding, burns, poisoning, a chemical release or a dose, and a Field Guide article matches it well, the app shows that article word for word and never asks the assistant. A person wrote the article and it names its manual. When no article matches, the app says so and points you to the packaging, a pharmacist or the manual instead of guessing.
Where does the content come from? Public sources under their own licences. Wikipedia and its medical wikis, government manuals in the public domain, the NHS, Stack Exchange. Most of the books are built by Kiwix. iFixit and MedlinePlus cannot be redistributed, so the app fetches them from Kiwix's own servers and marks them From Kiwix. The Sources page lists every title with its licence, size and edition.
Can I read the code? Yes. The app, its engine and ovsync are GPL-3.0 at github.com/nc/offlinevault , with the accuracy test and the Field Guide articles. The source page says what is where.
How do I activate? Pay with the button on a plan. The page after payment shows your licence key and an Open in OfflineVault button. Click it, or paste the key into Settings, Licence, Activate on each Mac. Core covers 2 Macs, Household and Founder 6.
I lost my key Enter the email you paid with at /recover . If that fails, reply to your Stripe receipt and we will send it again.
What Mac do I need? Apple Silicon, macOS 14 or later. 8 GB of memory runs the 4B model, 16 GB the 8B, 32 GB the 30B. The complete library wants an external SSD. Unplug the drive and the app waits for it. No Mac at all? ovsync downloads the same library for Kiwix on Linux or Windows.
OfflineVault
Terms Privacy Refunds Sources Accuracy Source Support 
Built on Kiwix, llama.cpp, MapLibre, OpenStreetMap, FFmpeg and yt-dlp. Map data from OpenStreetMap contributors.
Not medical, legal or safety advice. Read your sources and follow local authorities.

title: Show HN: Micron – The Oberon with the Power of C
author: Rochus
body:
# rochus-keller/Micron

A compiler and IDE for the Micron programming language - the Oberon with the power of C

- Stars: 77
- Forks: 7
- Watchers: 77
- Open issues: 1
- License: GNU General Public License v2.0
- Default branch: master
- Created: 2024-02-04T23:38:27Z

## Languages

- C
- C++
- Modula-2
- Pascal
- QMake
- Shell

## Top Contributors

- rochus-keller (215 contributions)

---

## README

This project implements a compiler for the Micron programming language.

Micron is a systems programming language with a syntax similar to Oberon+ and the flexibility of C. The name "Micron" is an abbreviation of "MicroOberon". 

Code examples can be found here; and here is the corresponding intermediate representation (text version).

The project is the result of the author's many years of work with the Oberon programming language and the analysis and migration of several versions of the Oberon system. It turned out that Oberon as such is in fact not particularly suitable for low-level and system-oriented programming, and that the systems mentioned could only be developed by direct memory manipulation and pointer arithmetic via SYSTEM module and other (partly undocumented) backdoors of the language, for large parts without the support of a type checker. 

The language of choice for such tasks is usually C, with which the author has been able to gain experience over many years and various projects and architectures down to different microcontrollers. A major advantage of C is its flexibility. The compiler provides fairly good support, but does not get in the way. However, C also has considerable disadvantages, such as the lack of modularization, the complications caused by the preprocessor, or the syntax that is by no means intuitive, just to name but a few. 

This project attempts to create a programming language and toolchain that combines the modularization, strictness and simplicity of Oberon with the power and flexibility of C. The language is aimed at experienced developers who know how to deal with the risks of direct memory and pointer manipulation. The preprocessor is replaced by language concepts that can largely substitute its features, supplemented by explicit support for generic programming, inlining and procedures that run at compile time. Thereby the focus is always on simplicity and the greatest effect with a practicable effort.
 
NOTE that this project is work-in-progress and not yet released for general use.

#### Planned features

- [x] Implement lexer with directive support
- [x] Implement parser and IR generator
- [x] Evaluate an existing compiler backend
- [x] Implement the analyzer/validator 
- [x] Implement a C99 generator
- [x] Implement an IDE with source navigation and debugger
- [x] Complete language and add explicit language levels
- [x] Implement a MIL interpreter for the full language scope (WIP)
- [x] Implement a native backend (WIP)
- [x] Migrate some notable C and Oberon projects to Micron as a proof-of-concept and to optimize the language (WIP)

#### Status on February 4, 2024

Generated a parser using the grammar and adopted the lexer from the Oberon project and the conditional compilation machinery from the Oberon and the FreePascal project. The parser is able to successfully read initial test files.

#### Status on February 20, 2024

Meanwhile I prepared a manual Micron parser and designed an intermediate language (see the grammar and the specification) which the Micron frontend will generate. There is also an automatically generated parser for the intermediate language which successfully works with initial test files.

#### Status on May 15, 2024

The programming and intermediate language have matured in parallel with the parser and code generator implementation. The IR code generator is integrated with the parser and operates in the same pass. Though not all parts of the language are yet supported by the IR generator (e.g. imports, VLAs and generics). Instead I was on a long quest for a suitable compiler backend that I could re-use for Micron (and other of my projects). The journey brought me to all sorts of toolkits and re-targetable compilers and I spent a lot of time studying and experimenting. There would be enough material for a treatise of its own. I also invested a lot of time in TCC, trying to modularize the code (that spaghetti lovers would be delighted with) and work out a minimal backend interface; I even started to add another frontend and had to grit my teeth over the TCC functionality, which - despite the introduction of modularization - turned out to be still almost incomprehensible. During this phase, user tarkonian drew my attention to the Eigen Compiler Suite, which looked very promising. After a thorough review of the large code base and excellent documentation, and an extensive exchange with the author, I came to the conclusion that Eigen is probably the best option currently available. It supports many more architectures than TCC (or e.g. QBE, Firm, , and the linker is also integrated (as with TCC), so you don't need any other dependencies, and the generated code is significantly faster than that of TCC. I also managed to make the relevant parts build with GCC 4.8 and MSVC 2015. The current focus is on implementing an Eigen IR generator for Micron; this will likely require more supporting activities (like e.g. an EBNF for the IR and translation examples with Oberon and C).

#### Status on December 18, 2025

The second year of the project is coming to an end, and a lot has happened. The language has matured in every aspect. We now have matured language levels, which optimize language 
features for different use cases, from low-level kernel and driver development up to high-level programming with support of a garbage collector, and which can be set per module. Significant expansions went into the type system and object-oriented capabilities (with IS operator and type case), interface types (similar to Go) and bound procedures for both records and objects, comprehensive support for generic programming through WHERE clauses and improved type constraints. There are now also bit fields (including packed variants), finally sections for resource cleanup (as a simple alternative for C++ destructors). Constructors became more flexible, allowing non-const and index components, and the @ operator now works with constructors. External interoperability improved with extern C declarations. Several features were removed for simplification: varargs support, symbol enums, and proc aliases.
Several large-scale refactorings improved code organization. And IDE was added, adopted from Oberon and Luon projects, integrating comprehensive cross-reference support covering all symbol uses. A MIL interpreter was integrated into the IDE with redirected output to IDE log and export capabilities for low-level bytecode. Most MIC/MIL features from the specification are implemented. The MIL interpreter underwent dramatic performance optimizations, so that it now achieves about 60% of Lua 5.4 (which of course is still too slow). Four distinct code generation backends for the MIL intermediate language have been implemented. The CeeGen (C generator) was fully completed and works with all testcases and AWFY. Experimental work began on EiGen, LLVM 4 IR, and CIL, though these remained work-in-progress.
A lot of time has been invested in the analysis of the Oberon System 3 and AOS/Bluebottle native implementations to assure that this code can be represented in Micron without the SYSTEM module tricks, loss of type checking, or inline assembler.

#### Precompiled versions

Not available at this time.

#### How to build

Qt Creator 3.x is currently used for development. There are *.pro files which are compatible with qmake, but there is no Qt dependency otherwise.
